speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

CHANGES IN CANADIAN DIPLOMATIC ESTABLISHMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe it was on Friday that the Prime Minister rebuked one of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party for listening to canards, paying attention to leaks and so on.
November 3, 1969

Diplomatic Establishment Changes What was a leak on Friday is, in fact, a communique on Monday.
I am impressed by the reference to cutbacks in operations in Latin America, recalling very well the loud blowing of trumpets when a certain ministerial group came back from that part of the world some months ago, and noting the reference in the Speech from the Throne to the intensification of Canada's contacts with the government and people of that area. I suppose there is some sort of inverse logic by which one could prove that curtailing the number of posts abroad might improve our contacts with the governments and peoples of foreign countries, but I would find that reasoning highly unflattering if I were a member of the Department of External Affairs. It would now seem to me that the prospect of this government leading Canada into the Organization of American States is very bleak at the present time.
It is not possible at this stage, in the proceedings on motions, to make a value judgment whether the closing of a post in Nicosia is a better move than the opening of one in Mauritius. These are matters which would have to be considered with greater care.
I am not sure I greet with happiness the reference to the International Control Commission. I have often thought there was a lack of faith in that organization and that as the Viet Nam war continued something much more effective might have been done, had there been the will, through the kind of grouping around which the ICC was involved. It strikes me that what we have noted today represents an abandonment of hope that this group can become more effective, that it is withering away and that, in fact, Canada's blessing has been given to this process.
I hope the minister's goals will be realized, but as to that we shall have to live in faith.

subsubtopic: CHANGES IN CANADIAN DIPLOMATIC ESTABLISHMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one can readily agree it is a desirable exercise to cut out any fat which can be removed from a department, and one would be readily disposed to consider the suggestions made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs had he gone a little further and told us precisely what he expects to save in terms of dollars and cents. It seems to me that the saving to the Canadian people and to the Canadian treasury as a result of the changes he has announced must be relatively small, even minimal, at a very considerable expense to Canada's role in the world. I hope the Standing Committee on External Affairs
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
and National Defence will take up the question of precisely how much is being saved by these changes.
I cannot find any fault, for example, with the decision to close the little office, as the minister calls it, in Berlin. Obviously the embassy in Bonn can deal with this responsibility. It seems to me, however, that to lessen our representation in Latin America at this time just does not make sense, particularly when we are attempting to improve our relations with Latin American countries.
As for the reference to the International Control Commissions, it occurs to me that at a time when the situation in southeast Asia is becoming more, rather than less, complex with the possible approach of peace, a country such as ours might well be taking on a bigger rather than a smaller role there, particularly when one bears in mind the problems confronting Laos through the presence of North Vietnamese and other military in that country. To eliminate entirely our representation in that part of the world, to say that our commissioner in Saigon will look after the situation while we still remain a member of the ICC, seems doubtful wisdom to me. I think hon. members would have to have proof that these savings were really important and could be substantiated before this kind of cutting down could be accepted with equanimity.
Before I was elected to parliament some years ago I lived in Ottawa for some time, and since I have been elected to parliament I have lived here most of the time. I have always been impressed by the fact that it took the Department of External Affairs at least a quarter of a century to build up a group of foreign service officers of very high calibre that compared favourably with that of any other country in the world. I express very profound doubt whether it is sensible to cut into this group of men and women who have represented Canada to great effect and with great credit. I end as I began, Mr. Speaker, by saying that we would have to be persuaded that the savings really justify this kind of myopic cutting down.

subtopic: DDT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEASURES TO CONTROL USE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: DDT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEASURES TO CONTROL USE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, an important objective of this government is the protection and enhancement of man's environment and, in harmony with this objective, the protection of man, crops and livestock from pests. One of the most successful pest control agents, DDT, has now been shown to have detrimental effects on the environment. Therefore I wish to make a statement on this pesticide.
We have studied the current data on the safety of DDT as it relates to human health and to its effects on wildlife, including fish. Our research shows that our environment is now widely contaminated with DDT residues. These residues are mostly at low levels but have concentrated sufficiently in a few populations of birds and fish to cause reproductive failures and the elimination of a few bird populations over large parts of their normal range. DDT applications have also caused direct kills of fish.
There is no evidence that present levels of DDT in the Canadian diet have caused injury to humans. Nevertheless, in the light of the persistence of DDT, its deleterious effects on wildlife, and lack of clearcut evidence about its long-term effects on man, it is prudent to curtail contamination of the environment by it.
Within the Government, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) administers the Pest Control Products Act which regulates pesti-
Measures to Control Use of Pesticides cides offered for sale to assure that they are effective and safe when used as labelled. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) administers the Food and Drugs Act which has as one of its major objectives the assurance that foods do not contain pesticide residues at levels in excess of those established as safe for lifetime consumption.
[DOT] (11:20 a.m.)

The government has taken action in recent years to limit the amount of DDT used by federal agencies.
Hon. members probably know, that two years ago we discontinued the use of DDT in the protection of forests. In 1968 we eliminated the use of DDT in national parks and by 1969 aerial use by the armed forces. We have now completed a year-long review of the overall use pattern of formulations accepted for registration for sale under the Pest Control Products Act. After January 1, 1970, DDT will not be registered for insect and biting fly control in forests, parks, and other outdoor areas except under emergency situations and only after careful consulta ion between federal and provincial interdepartmental committees.
In addition, whereas in 1969 DDT was registered for the control of insects on 62 food crops, in 1970 registration will be granted under the Pest Control Products Act for use on only 12 agricultural crops. It is estimated that all these actions will reduce the amount of DDT used by at least 90 per cent. The remaining uses of DDT will be retained until prac'ical, safe replacement compounds or other protective measures are available.
The federal government, of course, recognizes and commends the partial controls already implemented by some provinces. It was felt, however, that more comprehensive and unified action was required at this time.
Concomitant with the revised use pattern we are, under the Food and Drugs Act, reducing the tolerance for DDT from seven parts per million to one part per million for 61 common vegetables and fruits such as beans, carrots, corn, lettuce, peas, tomatoes, strawberries, and all citrus fruits. For apples, pears, and celery, the DDT tolerance will be reduced to three and a half parts per million. The only tolerance for DDT that will remain unchanged at seven parts per million is for the fat of the meat of cattle, hogs and sheep. This tolerance will be further reduced or eliminated when practical replacement compounds are available to us and our trading
November 3, 1969

Measures to Control Use of Pesticides partners. There are no tolerances for DDT in potatoes and no tolerances for any pesticide residues in eggs, fish, milk, butter, cheese, ice cream and other dairy products. Our goal will be to effect further reductions in some of these tolerances and to eliminate others.
Bon appetit, Mr. Speaker!

Lest you are concerned about the levels of DDT in food, I think you should know that the Food and Agriculture and World Health Organizations of the United Nations, on the advice of expert scientific groups, have declared maximum acceptable daily intakes for humans on the basis of ingestion for a lifetime. For DDT, the recommended maximum daily acceptable intake is 0.7 milligrams. The average Canadian diet contains less than 5 per cent of this amount and food contributes 80 per cent to 90 per cent of the total intake of DDT by the general public.
In concluding this announcement I wish to emphasize that our scientists are world leaders in research toward the minimal but effective use of chemicals in pest control. This government will continue to examine all scientific evidence and intensify its own research program into pesticides, including organo-chlorine and other persistent compounds. The government of Canada will continue to play a leading international role in moves to protect and enhance man's total environment.
To this end, Canada has been an active member of international organizations, the role of which is to develop international standards for pesticides based on sound health and ecological principles and the needs of international trade. Canada will continue and will intensify its work in these organizations.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: DDT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEASURES TO CONTROL USE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome in general this move announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). A good many of us, and I think the country generally, have been quite concerned about the effects of DDT upon our environment, our wildlife and eventually upon human health ever since reading that very striking book written by the late Rachel Carson some years ago. I believe a few years ago following that book and other publications a committee of the House conducted an investigation into this subject.
I am a little disturbed, because of the duration of time over which public concern has been expressed, that the government appears

to be following rather than leading. I hope one can really place firm reliance upon the assurances given by the Prime Minister concerning the efforts Canadian scientists and the Canadian government are to make in the future with regard to pesticides generally, their safety and environmental effects.
I am also a little surprised by what I take to be the implication in the Prime Minister's announcement that it is only during the past year that the government has been conducting in any sense a full-scale examination of the environmental effects of the use of DDT. It was announced that it had been decided, I think in 1968, not to use DDT in our own forests and parks and in 1969 the aerial use by the armed forces was stopped. But the Prime Minister said that the government has now completed a year long review of the over-all use pattern of formulations acceptable for registration. I may say, if this means what it seems to mean, I am shocked that it is only over the past year the government has been conducting in a serious way an examination of the over-all use.
There have been a number of indications lately of the care with which miracle pesticides and miracle substitutes must be examined, and there has been a growing concern about the way in which we are polluting our environment by, among other methods, using pesticides which have very profound residual effects. So generally I welcome the announcement and hope it means that the government of Canada is really going to take a sustained interest in and conduct an examination of such pesticides and substitutes.
I am a little concerned with regard to what consultation has taken place with farm organizations and what the effect of this announcement will be on agriculture when it has to turn quickly to certain substitutes. I would like to hope there has been some consultation with the provinces which have an interest in the effect on their agricultural industry.
Above all, I do not see any indication in the statement by the Prime Minister that the government has really been placing the emphasis it should have been placing upon the development of substitutes which would have a satisfactory cost effectiveness so far as our farmers are concerned. Certainly there is no mention of consultation with the provinces, particularly the provincial departments of agriculture. I hope that in fact there has been such consultation. In view of the difficulty many forms of agriculture are facing, I hope a really determined effort is being made to
November 3, 1969

develop satisfactory pesticide substitutes with appropriate cost effectiveness.
[DOT] (11:30 a.m.)
Having said this, having placed emphasis upon the need for consultation with the provinces, I also note that in the Prime Minister's statement there is no assurance that all departments of the government will comply with bans imposed by the provinces. I express very fervently the hope that all federal departments will in fact comply with general bans on the use of DDT imposed by any province and that the Prime Minister will be prepared to give such an assurance.
However, with these caveats-I do not want to be misunderstood in any sense-I certainly welcome the statement by the Prime Minister and his announcement that these steps are being taken to cut down the use of DDT very substantially. I only hope that the lesson that has been learned will in fact encourage the government and its departments to have a sharper eye in the future for difficulties of this sort, and to give the problem, in co-operation with other countries, its most urgent and effective attention.

subtopic: DDT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEASURES TO CONTROL USE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our group certainly welcomes the statement made by the Prime Minister this morning in regard to DDT. However, I feel, as did the previous speaker, that action of this type is long overdue. Frankly, I have been amazed at the lengthy delay in government action on this important matter. It has been the work of the provinces and other groups which have done a vast amount of research into the dangers of pesticides that has really forced the issue so far as the government is concerned.
I can recall asking a question three months ago of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) regarding DDT and its effect on foods so far as Canadians are concerned. We were assured at that time that there was no danger and nothing to worry about. Three months later we find that the government has decided to take action and ban the use of DDT in certain cases.
I think it is only fair to point out that the Prime Minister has indicated that other research is going on into other types of pesticides because there are a number of toxic pesticides that are just as dangerous as DDT. A number of reports-I have a couple on my desk-some of them over a year old, have been prepared by wildlife associations in the United States which point out that a group of very dangerous pesticides, which have been and are being used today in the United
Measures to Control Use of Pesticides States, Canada and other countries in the world, is having a bad effect on our environment. There is no doubt that in some cases the effects certainly are not as bad as those of DDT but they are traceable, and we find that practically all living organisms in every part of the world have some trace of these pesticides in them. It seems to me that Canadian research facilities to study these problems have been inadequate.
As I said, the action taken by the government now is a step forward and our group certainly welcomes it. But may I point out to the Prime Minister and the government that this is just one small phase of the pollution problem. Just a week or two ago we received a report dealing with detergents containing phosphorus. Two years is suggested as the time to be allowed before the production of detergents containing phosphorus must stop. I suggest to the government that this is another phase of pollution which must be tackled without delay. Research must go forward to ensure, when a change is made by these companies in the manufacturing of their various products, that a suitable product is substituted. There are other aspects of pollution with which I will not deal at present, such as pollution of the atmosphere which must not be allowed to continue much longer. Again in this case we have a report prepared by the United Nations dealing with the inherent dangers to mankind unless we move quickly.
I congratulate the government on this initial move, and I urge that a whole series of investigations be made to deal with the series of grave pollution problems at present threatening the very existence of mankind.

Ontario and Quebec having recently taken a stand in that matter, the federal government has finally decided to act.

An important objective of my government is the protection and enhancement of man's environment and, in harmony with this objective, the protection of man, crops, and livestock from pests.

November 3, 1969

From that you might think that the government has always cared about that matter, whereas it is well known that it is taking action at last only under pressure from other governments, that is the provincial governments.
Needless to say, we are not blaming the federal government for taking some action, but we are blaming it for sometimes doing it only when it feels that it cannot do otherwise, when it wishes to be ahead of the others or to take credit for having taken the initiative. I hope that the minister will take note of these comments and will make sure that the necessary funds are made available to that association for the pursuit of its goals.
Mr. Speaker, I think that all hon. members agree that the real solution to poverty is to improve our education system so as to prevent our young people from prematuraly leaving school or university.
As to those who are too old to go back to school or university, it is a good thing that they take advantage of the retraining programs of the Department of Manpower and Immigration. But in spite of that, there will remain a group of people between the ages of 40 and 60 who can neither go back to school nor take part in the retraining program. What should be done with these people, for it is where the real problem of poverty lies?
I think we should resort to social development. Those people should be informed so that they will become aware of their problems. It would not solve anything to tell them: coastal fishing is bound to disappear and you will be requested to move to the city, or you will have to undergo retraining.
These people must truly become aware of their problems, and, to a certain extent, become masters of their own destiny.
I would like to mention the excellent job being done to this end by various organizations: the Professional Association of Fishermen and the Northern Regional Development

Council. I hope that they will always be able to rely on the support of the various levels of government.

In my opinion, we should consider the aim of the Company of Young Canadians, its structure and the kind of people working within it
I was both surprised and distressed, Mr. Speaker, when I heard the charges laid by Mr. Saulnier against the Company of Young Canadians. This group was specifically set up by the federal government to help the poor and the underprivileged to organize themselves and to settle their problems in a more satisfactory way.
It seems quite possible that those people will form within society, a group and perhaps resort to violence, because they have been overlooked in the past by the various government levels. They have been rejected by the Canadian society. They are truly alienated. No decision has been taken by the government in this connection. Those people are not strong enough to assert themselves.
Yet, when other segments of our population are affected by some government decision, they can resort to lobbying and try and influence the administration.
But, what course can the poor and the underprivileged citizens take since they are never consulted? Sometimes they resort to violence.
I really regret that such a serious administration as that of Montreal should have made demagogic charges, just taking advantage of the conditions that prevailed in the city, while people were nervous after several days of violence, and blamed the Company of Young Canadians.

Why did Mr. Saulnier not ask the police to stop such disorders? If there are any subversive activities in another

organization in Montreal, will he not send the police there to inquire? No, what he wanted was to destroy the Company of Young Canadians. As for myself, I feel differently. Those who make such charges do not want social animation. They cannot accept it.
The Liberal party in New Brunswick, for instance, was threatened-and so was I because I was a member of it-by those who were doing social animation. This might not bring an immediate solution to the unemployment problem in our area or improve the socio-economic standard of living of these people, but at least they will be encouraged to take small risks and get their businesses off to a good start.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to congratulate the two members responsible for the
The Address-Mr. Danforth moving and seconding the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. Normally Speeches from the Throne do not create a great deal of interest on the part of the citizens of Canada. Normally corporation lawyers and small businessmen have knowledgeable partners who pursue the substance of Speeches from the Throne in order to have some indication of the government's intentions in respect of the business and financial world and how the legislation proposed will affect directly their own businesses. But I earnestly feel the situation was just a little different this year. I believe that Canadians as a whole were very much concerned about the Speech from the Throne and were very much interested in what it might contain because over the past months the ordinary Canadian has become increasingly alarmed about the future of this country.
The ordinary Canadian has been faced with the highest cost of living in Canadian history; he has been faced with the highest interest rates in Canadian history; he has been faced with the highest tax rates in Canadian history. He is aware that we have the highest national debt in our history and is finding that the new measures chosen by the government to curb inflation tend to stagnate business and cause an ever-increasing trend toward the highest unemployment in Canadian history. So I contend that the citizens of Canada were more concerned about the Speech from the Throne this year than in any previous year.
As a country we are approaching a new decade with perhaps more basic knowledge at our command than ever before and more instruments and tools with which to work for the welfare of human beings world-wide and in Canada than ever before in the history of man. Therefore this speech was anticipated on two grounds. It was anticipated, first, because of the basic troubles facing the country and the hope that a solution might be presented and pursued in the ensuing ten years. I

The Address-Mr. Danforth think the lack of attendance by members in the House, the lack of attendance in the press gallery and the lack of attendance in the public gallery are a terrible and solemn condemnation of the failure of the Speech from the Throne to generate specific enthusiasm on the part of the people of Canada or to portray any hope for the future.

speechtext:
Even the members of the press, those keen students of political science, in trying to wade through the chaff and pick out the kernels are finding it particularly difficult to discover in the Speech from the Throne any basic interest or principle for the Canadian public. When the press of this nation have to concentrate on two main points in the Speech from the Throne, first, that the voting age of citizens of Canada will be reduced to 18 years and, second, that perhaps the Speech from the Throne will become famous for what it did not say rather than for what it did say, this is an indication to me and my colleagues of how difficult they find it to accept this Speech from the Throne.
We who sit in opposition in parliament and the people of Canada must try to convince the government that the time has now come to deal with some of the desperate problems facing Canada today. No longer can we accept platitudes, alibis and excuses. No longer can we accept statements that discussions are under way, investigations are taking place, task forces are about to report and something will be done after consultation. During the past 18 months we have found these statements to be mere verbiage; they do not mean anything. The people of Canada are becoming well aware that this government would rather see important questions bogged down in excess verbiage than take serious steps in order to create an atmosphere in which a solution might be forthcoming.
I criticize the Prime Minister of this country, although not as an individual because I feel every member of this House is entitled to his own personal life. The Prime Minister, however, certainly represents the image of this country and in effect is the leading parliamentary figure in Canada. So his actions have a direct bearing on every phase of Canadian life. That is why I express concern today about his actions.
When this Parliament began the Prime Minister seemed intent not only on ascertaining what the problems are but on dealing

with them by direct dialogue with the people of Canada, with a frank and honest exchange of views, in order that all might participate in what he termed "the just society." I feel that this ideology, this concept of participatory politics, is to be commended. Environmental politics appeal to people of all classes. We soon learned from actions in the House, however, that what seemed to be an ideal was not to be the order of business by the government controlling Canada today. When a Prime Minister who insists on direct dialogue with the people of Canada must hold a special caucus of his own party in Ottawa because of a lack of direct dialogue with his own backbenchers this gives an indication of how he has failed to promote dialogue among the people of the country.
It would seem to me that a man intent on convincing members of this House and the people of the nation of his serious intentions should provide an image so that we could follow his example. But what do we find? We find that this man who speaks of direct dialogue has in his own office many men engaged in specialized services in the role of assistants, executive assistants, secretaries to assistants and secretaries to secretaries. The list grows longer and longer. As a matter of fact as an indication of just how cumbersome his office has become there is a division into regions and there are regional desks designated to control the welfare of areas across Canada. Does it not seem strange that the Prime Minister despite the presence of Liberal backbenchers representing Canadians feels the need to institute such an establishment in order to find out what is going on in the various constituencies rather than consulting his own members.

In my own field of agriculture legislation was brought forward with the primary purpose of lending to the young farmers of this nation ample funds to consolidate and increase their holdings into so-called economic units. However, that was last session. This session the emphasis is on cutting down the subsidies to agriculture and the moneys poured into the agricultural field. The result is that these young men are faced with a curtailment of trade and production, a lack of sales and a tightening of credit. This is forcing them into a position where there is no other future but bankruptcy. They cannot survive on what was provided for them last year having regard to the economic climate provided for them this year. This is a direct contradiction in policy.
In another field we have heard over and over again Ministers of Finance stand in their

The Address-Mr. Danforth place and say that the future of Canada depends on increased productivity. As productivity increases our gross national product increases and so does our over-all economy. What do we see now? We see direct government action designed to cool off the economy of Canada-I think that was the wording used-and we see a tight money policy designed to decrease productivity and increase unemployment or bring about a slack in employment in order to create an atmosphere in which the government says that it can fight inflation. This is in direct contradiction of the policy that was in effect some months ago. As a matter of fact, what has alarmed members of the opposition in all parties is the contention on the part of government members month after month that Canadians have never had it so good, in spite of our protestations that we were in trouble with inflation and a higher cost and decreased standard of living. Then we have another contradiction, which was mentioned by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. McCutcheon), with regard to the committee system of Parliament. This seems to be their prime objective. If they were successful in their contention and right in their intent regarding Parliament, this House would be filled with members and would resound with debate. We would have the political cross-fire for which Canadians throughout the ages have been noted. Mr. Speaker, at the time of adjournment I was dealing with some of the inadequacies of the Throne Speech, and with the sorry state in which we find parliament today. Parliament certainly has not the image that it should have in Canada and among the nations. It no longer has the prestige that it should have in Canada and among the nations. And certainly, it no longer has the influence that it should have in Canada and among the nations. The whole responsibility for this deterioration can be laid solely at the feet of the present government.
When a parliamentary career is begun by requesting at least half of the ministers not to attend in the House on particular days, thus making it impossible for them to answer questions from opposition members on the workings of their departments, it is not conducive to the fulfilment of the full-time parliamentary obligations of all hon. members. Ministers not only have the opportunity to be the heads of departments but share the obligations of other hon. members to be full-time representatives of those people who chose to send them to Ottawa to look after their interests. I am sure the leader of my party would be in dire difficulty if at any time he even insinuated that a member of this party should not attend every sitting of the House.
It does not do parliament any good when policy statements are not presented on motions, but are made in the halls of parliament to television and press representatives, with no opportunity accorded to members of the House to criticize and point out the weaknesses in announced policies. This happens time and time again. We now find that newspapers, by means of so-called leaks, are able to obtain indications of government policy sometimes days in advance of that policy being announced in this House. This does not do the prestige, influence and image of parliament one bit of good.
The Speech from the Throne afforded an opportunity to demonstrate Canada's intentions in many areas. At one time Canadians were world leaders in many fields. No one can forget the effect that the discovery of insulin had in helping the diabetics of the world. No one can forget the pioneering work done by Canadians with uranium, particularly the first reactors that were constructed in Canada. These were outstanding events. No one can forget the tremendous work done in [The Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard).]
Canada in the fields of plant breeding, animal genetics and in the use of chemicals. No one can forget the work done in Canada to perfect machinery for production. No one can forget the high productivity levels reached through the efforts of Canadian management, unions and other labour groups.
Now, we are no longer leaders. Under this administration it seems that we only follow. We did not do anything about tobacco and its alleged evil effects until other countries had demonstrated the ills that could flow from the use of tobacco. We did not become aware of the danger of cyclamates in foods until another country discovered it. What are we doing to investigate saccharine? Look at our delay in taking steps to meet the DDT problem. We should be giving leadership in these areas instead of following others. We know what the problems are, yet nothing is done about them.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
The people of Canada had every right to believe that in the Throne Speech the government would enunciate a solid, comprehensive program to deal with the problems facing the nation today, problems of pullution, problems of inflation, problems of poverty, problems of housing, and the serious and ever-growing problem of drug addiction among young people in Canada. It is my considered opinion that members of the opposition and the people of Canada generally will not be satisfied with verbiage, platitudes, white papers, investigations and other time consuming and delaying actions on the part of this government. The people of Canada demand, and have the right to demand, that their parliament act. Members of the opposition are just as determined to see that this shall happen. Nowhere does the Speech from the Throne say exactly what the government intends to do. As a result of our questioning and our prodding, we must force this government to take that action on behalf of the people of Canada that we feel is necessary and justified in order that Canada may once again take her rightful place among the community of nations.
An examination of legislation proposed during the previous session reveals that that legislation seemed to be social legislation only. It dealt with the climate of ever increasing permissiveness in society. In the ten years ahead of us, we have the opportunity to make a name for Canada. Why should Canadians not deal directly with problems facing
November 3, 19G9

Canada and the world. I am, of course, referring to those problems I have outlined. Why can we not do that instead of dealing with nebulous bills and legislation designed, it seems, to degrade and break down the essentials of human dignity or, in the alternative, to eradicate in this House and throughout Canada the defenseless symbols of English influence. Certainly, the time has come when we must act on behalf of the people of Canada. That the government has such intention is not evident in the Speech from the Throne.
The mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne have my warmest admiration and my greatest sympathy. Having read how little the legislation outlined in the Speech from the Throne will deal with matters that are of vital importance to Canadians today, I request hon. members present, one and all, to reject this Speech from the Throne.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Davis (Minister of Fisheries and Forestry):
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members on both sides of the House have been unanimous in praising the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I, too, would like to congratulate our two new members of parliament for the way in which they have enlivened our proceedings at the beginning of this debate. They both saw a great deal of merit in the government's program for the coming session, and for this I commend them heartily.
This year's Speech from the Throne is notable for several reasons. It is wide-ranging in the sense that it provides us with a backdrop against which to assess the government's priorities. It is also informative in that it defines important issues and mentions major pieces of legislation. One of the foremost issues which it defines is pollution. Another is the extension of Canada's jurisdiction seaward from our shores. Both these subjects, of course, are vital to our fisheries.
In my remarks today I want to take you a bit farther. I want to talk about fisheries and about Canada's own fishing limits. I want to say a word about the effect of pollution on our marine life and I want to draw your attention to the damage which large foreign fishing fleets are doing to our nearby fishing grounds in the North Atlantic and in the Pacific as well. Man is learning to manage his affairs in many fields of endeavour. But in respect of fishing we have a long, long way to go.
The Address-Mr. Davis
True, we are beginning to manage our living resources in an intelligent manner. We are assessing fish populations and estimating maximum sustainable yields. We are trimming our fishing fleets down to size and increasing the income of the average Canadian fisherman. But all of this is of no avail if industrial wastes on the one hand, and foreign fishing fleets on the other, are paying scant regard to sound conservation practice. This is why we have a number of pieces of new legislation, new fisheries legislation, to deal with during the coming session. This is why we will have more legislation next year and the year after that, legislation which will not only increase the value of our commercial and sports fisheries but also help to protect the living resources of the northern hemisphere as well.
Several hon. members opposite have been talking as if we didn't have anything to offer in the fisheries field. Obviously, they have not read the Speech from the Throne carefully; that or only the first few pages. Rarely, if ever, has a government program contained so many references to this vital sector of our economy. Rarely has a government had so many fisheries bills to introduce.
Perhaps I should list the main ones now. They are, first, the Fisheries Act, which is to be amended; second, the Salt Fish Development Act, which is new legislation; third, the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act, which is to be amended and, fourth, the Territorial Seas and Fishing Zones Act, which is to be amended. I could add to this list the Canada Water Act, because that is a new act which will deal with pollution from coast to coast, and the proposed changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act. The question of unemployment insurance is of great interest to our fishermen as hon. members know.
Anyone interested in Canada's fisheries can have a field day on any one of these pieces of legislation. However we are looking for action and above all we are looking for suggestions. No good suggestion from whatever source will be ignored. We want to do the best we can for our own fishermen and the thoughts of any hon. member or any hon. member's ideas for action will be considered seriously I can assure you.
The government is proposing to do things, a good many things. It is proposing to re-organize our fisheries on both coasts, in the Arctic and in our inland waters. By legislating on pollution we will be protecting the resource itself. And by defining our fishing limits we

November 3, 1969
The Address-Mr. Davis will be improving our competitive position internationally as well.
After listening to some members opposite talking about the good old days I became curious. I checked up on what happened when the Conservative Party was in power. What did the Speeches from the Throne say between 1957 and 1962 when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) introduced seven Speeches from the Throne. Four Speeches from the Throne out of the seven didn't mention fisheries at all. Two others merely said that provisions in old bills passed by the preceding Liberal administration would be continued for a few more years. Only one had a whole paragraph on the fisheries. It was the first of the seven and it was followed by no legislation whatsoever.
And what by contrast do I find in the Speech from the Throne today? I find all sorts of references about the fisheries, about pollution, and about the protection of our resources offshore. I see references to fish life in the Arctic, references to international agreements and referencs to new fish marketing arrangements. What more can hon. members ask than that?
Fishing in other words is being upgraded by the present government. It is being looked at for what it is, part of our total ecology. We see it as one renewable resource among many, a resource along with wildlife, trees and water itself; a renewable resource the protection of which is essential to the future health and prosperity of mankind. In the present Speech from the Throne, the speech before you outlining the government's program for 1969-1970 I read this:
The competitive position of Canada's fisheries must also be strengthened ... by extending Canada's exclusive fishing zones.
This by itself is an important announcement. It emphasizes the government's intention to finish the job of defining Canada's exclusive fishing zones. To this end you will be asked to amend Canada's Territorial Seas and Fishing Zones Act. You will be asked to include a clause defining a new concept-that of "fisheries closing lines". We will be asking this House in other words for authority to complete the fisheries map of Canada, the map showing where Canadians alone can fish and where we alone can say exactly what happens to our marine biota as a living resource.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
Those of you who are familiar with fisheries matters know that we have a 12-mile

limit. We have had a 12-mile exclusive fishing zone ever since 1964. Before that it was three miles the same as our present territorial sea. The first three miles out, in other words, are part of the territory of Canada. The next nine miles are part of our exclusive fishing zone. That was the rule, and that zone followed the ins and outs of our coasts until we drew "baselines", and the idea of "baselines", or lines from headland to headland, was also contained in the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act of 1964.
The government began to draw its first baselines in 1967. It drew them from headland to headland down the east coast of Labrador and around the eastern and southern coasts of Newfoundland. This spring it drew other baselines down the east coast of Nova Scotia and up off the west coasts of Vancouver Island and the Queen Charlottes. As a result, we have closed numerous bays and inlets to foreign fishermen. Not only that, but we have a 12-mile limit extending seaward from the headland to headland lines, or baselines, which we have already published on our fisheries maps for all to see.
There are still a number of important gaps in our 12-mile fisheries lines. These gaps can easily be spotted on our maps. They include the Strait of Belle Isle and Cabot Strait in the mouth of the Gulf of St. Lawrence. They include the Bay of Fundy, also on the east coast, the Queen Charlotte Sound and Hecate Strait on the west coast.
Generally speaking, these are wider waters, longer distances, bigger gaps, than those which we have spanned with our baselines. There is, for instance, a 56 mile gap across the Cabot Strait between Newfoundland and Nova Scotia and a 94 mile gap across Queen Charlotte Sound off British Columbia. Here is where the concept of fisheries closing lines applies. Here is where we, again, must distinguish between Canadian territorial waters on the one hand and Canadian exclusive fishing zones on the other.
I say "distinguish" because Canada took the lead among the nations of the world in separating the fishing concept from the territorial waters concept, separating the fishing zone idea from the territorial waters idea, more than a decade ago. We said that our fishing limits should extend 12 miles out to sea, while our territorial waters remained at three miles. At first there was considerable opposition, internationally, to this idea, but the Canadian view prevailed in the long run. Now, many
November 3, 1969	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Davis countries, including the United States, have a three mile territorial limit and a 12-mile fishing limit.
Now, we are pushing for a series of "fisheries closing lines". We are pushing for "closing lines" which will apply to fishing and fishing alone. We want to be able, for instance, to regulate and conserve our fisheries in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. We want to do this under Canadian law. Having drawn a fisheries closing line across the Strait of Belle Isle and the Cabot Strait, we will be able to keep foreign fishermen out. Not only that, but we will and can apply the anti-pollution provisions of our Fisheries Act, which will be improved by amendments this session. When the fisheries closing lines are drawn the Fisheries Act will apply to the whole Gulf of St. Lawrence. We will be able to protect the marine, animal and vegetable life in the Gulf and do this without let or hindrance from others.
To repeat, the concept of a "fisheries closing line" is new to the field of international law. It is new, as our 12 mile concept was a decade or so ago. It is a line related to fisheries only; to the ecology of the area. It is a line defining what is, and what is not, the exclusive fishing zone of Canada. Inside the line we can regulate and protect marine life.
Outside of it, on the other hand, our fishermen are still in a sort of no man's land, a land where few rules apply and where overfishing on the part of many nations threatens to upset the ecological balance over great areas of our continental shelf. This will not be true within our exclusive fishing zones where we will have full control over pollution, fishing and the like.
Within these new and well-defined exclusive fishing zones of Canada we will be able to do a number of things. We will be able to protect the resource using an amended Fisheries Act. We will be able to deal with pollution, more effectively, from land based plants, from ships and from oil drilling rigs. We will also be able to tailor our fishing capacity so as to fit the resource. We will be able to conserve and to operate on the basis of a sustained yield. We will be able to exploit our marine biota, animal and vegetable, to the maximum while, at the same time, keeping an eye on the long term future. We, in other words, will be able to manage and conserve the resources within our exclusive fishing zones, zones which, thanks to baselines, the "fishing closing line" concept and the 12-mile limit will be continuous around our coasts.

So far, I have said little about the north. But the same laws and the same concepts should apply in Canada's Arctic. One might visualize, in the fullness of time, a sequence of fisheries lines forming a complete umbrella over Canada's great Arctic archipelago. They would stretch from our northernmost island down to Alaska in the west, and down to Labrador in the east. They would create a great and varied Canadian exclusive fishing zone in the north, and the pollution control provisions of our Fisheries Act would apply there as well. They would apply as much to the plankton as to the walrus and the polar bear. They would apply as much to the seal, the Arctic char and the northern cod, as to the various forms of vegetable life which grow, more slowly, it is true, in the great seas, straits and inlets, Canadian seas, straits and inlets, in this great Canadian northland of ours.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that I am making myself clear in one important respect at least. I am not talking about territorial waters. I am not talking about navigation. I am talking, essentially, about the protection and management of our living environment. I am talking about the intelligent management of our living resource of the sea. I am talking about animal life, vegetable life and Canadian laws in exclusive Canadian fishing zones.
This life we must protect at all costs. We must protect it while, at the same time, allowing other people to come and go without undue hindrance or loss. I am not talking about territorial waters so much as exclusive fishing zones. I am not talking about transportation in the wider sense of the word. I am talking about conservation and the intelligent harvesting of living resources. I am not talking about hindering mobility. I am talking about a healthier ecology. We always want to maximize our mobility-and that of other people. We must at the same time protect the living environment, the ecology of all of Canada and its adjoining seas.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like hon. members to look even farther afield; to look out even farther from our shores; to look even farther into the future to see what it holds for our fishermen and ourselves. I want them to look out to the limits of our continental shelf and beyond. I want them to think, not only in terms of straight baselines and exclusive fishing zones, but also of the natural habitat of much of our fish life. I want them to recognize the fact that fish, being highly mobile animals, are no respecters of manmade boundaries. They will continue to swim

back and forth across Canada's man-made fishing lines. It follows that, in order to manage our fishery resources intelligently, we will often have to look out to the edge of the continental shelf itself, out to the limits of our Grand Banks in the east and the edge of the great deeps in the west. We will have to look at the living quarters of each of our major fish species, the geography, and the whole of their habitat. We will have, in other words, to concern ourselves about the state of the living resource, the living marine resource, the whole area of the seas adjacent to our shores, the seas beyond our exclusive fishing zones.
We have every right to do so, Mr. Speaker. That right is enshrined in the articles adopted by the international conference on the law of the sea back in 1958. Article I reads:
All states have the right for their nationals to engage in fishing on the high seas, subject ... to the interests and rights of coastal states . . . and to articles concerning conservation of the living resources of the high seas.
Article VI goes even further. It states that:
A coastal state has a special interest in the maintenance of the productivity of the living resources in any area of the high seas adjacent to its territorial sea.
Article VII takes us a step further. It goes so far as to say that:
Any coastal state may, with a view to the maintenance of the productivity of the living resources of the sea, adopt unilateral measures of conservation appropriate to any stock of fish or other marine resources in any area of the high seas adjacent to its territorial sea, provided that negotiations to that effect with the other states concerned have not led to an agreement within six months.
This all sounds clear enough. But what has really happened in the North Atlantic? What is happening today in the North Pacific? Gigantic, foreign fleets are moving in. The total fishing effort is going up. Fish stocks, many of which are already threatened, are going down. Productivity is dropping off. Some species are already over-fished, and the fate of our inshore fishermen, our Canadian inshore fishermen, is in the balance. Already the scales are tipped heavily against these Canadian fishermen. There is little they alone can do to restore runs of fish along our shores or raise their income from fishing, no matter how hard they try.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
What, really, has happened in the North Atlantic for instance? The total fishing effort, the international fishing effort, has more than

fleets have moved in and, while the total catch has gone up, the catch per unit of effort has gone down. The big, foreign state-owned fleets are not as productive as our own Canadian fishermen, but they catch a lot of fish.
A recent report of the Atlantic Development Board tells us that the productivity of Canadian vessels is much higher than that of the big Russian ships operating in the North Atlantic. Their catch per hour was only about 60 per cent of the Newfoundland catch per hour in 1960 and today it is only about 40 per cent of the catch taken per hour by our Newfoundland fishermen. In other words, these big foreigners do not catch as many pounds of fish per man day at sea as our vessels do. Their top officials are frank to admit that the economics of their long-range fishing effort are suspect by western standards. The fact is that they continue to throw these massive fleets at us, fleets of 50 or more vessels each in which the length of the average vessel ranges upwards of 200 feet.

speechtext: Can the minister indicate the volume ratio as between foreign and domestic vessels as far as catches are concerned?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
On the east coast-I am talking about the North Atlantic-the Canadian fishing fleet now takes about one third of the total groundfish catch whereas we took about one half ten years ago. This gives an idea of the relative fishing effort.
During the past summer I flew over a Russian fleet just outside the 12-mile limit off the west coast of Vancouver Island. It consisted of 40 giant trawlers, every one of which was bigger than a B.C. ferry. At night the fleet looked like a city, all lit up in the distance. It was indeed a small city, in that it was manned by at least 5,000 Russians. And it stayed there, close by our Canadian fishing limits, for many days. Dragging gigantic nets backward and forward over a few square miles off our coast it cleaned off one of our most productive fishing grounds. It can clean it off, not just for months, but for many years to come. And, mark you, there are many such fleets working their way up and down our coasts. They are cutting into our marine resources in a truly massive way. They are hitting our fishing industry hard, and they are hitting our resources hard. They are hitting them so hard that many of them may never recover.
November 3, 1969

Important species have been knocked back to the point where they are of little commercial interest to Canadians. Haddock from the east coast is a case in point. Ocean perch over the shelf areas of the North Pacific may soon be another. This is exploitation with a vengeance, and it has to stop.
I might elaborate. Whereas the maximum haddock catch in 1965 was of the order of 250,000 metric tons in the North Atlantic it is now approximately 100,000 metric tons a year at the maximum. On the west coast, the result of a day's catching effort in terms of groundfish is now 40 per cent of what it was five years ago. In both cases, big foreign fleets have been very active and the reduction in yield indicates what the effect on the resources has been.
Here is what a recent British report had to say about the situation in the North Atlantic:
There is no doubt that the general decline In stock abundance is, in the main, due to fishing pressures. Although the international catch, in total, is as high as ever, the catch per unit of effort has fallen substantially, with the effect that some fishing units are no longer economic.
The report states further:
In some stocks the level of production could actually be improved by reducing the amount of fishing, so that, for the purpose of obtaining the maximum amount of protein for the minimum amount of fishing effort, there is much to be said for some control of the amount of fishing.
Our own Canadian studies, meanwhile, show that the tonnage of fish caught per hour has continued to drop. It has dropped sharply over the past decade. The Russian effort, although it is only roughly half as productive as our own per man day, has increased nearly fivefold. And, according to the Atlantic Development Board, "the fact that the Canadian fleet is more than twice as efficient as their own obviously has no bearing on the Russian decision to fish. What is more significant is that the increased effort by other nations has led to a decline in Canadian return per unit of effort."
In groundfish, our share has dropped from roughly half of the total ten years ago to about a third at the present time. Our inshore fishermen, meanwhile, are catching fewer fish. Productivity, in terms of pounds per man day, has been cut roughly in half. This, really, expresses the fate of many of our inshore fishermen, particularly of those who live in Newfoundland. They are catching half as many fish now as they did in the 'fifties. It is true prices have risen but they have not risen sufficiently to offset increases in their
21362-21 i
The Address-Mr. Davis costs. In other words, their real income has tended to decline over the past decade in marked contrast to the rise in living standards of most Canadians.
This drop in productivity, like the failure of our Labrador fishery this year, can be attributed largely to an excessive offshore effort, an excessive offshore effort not only by big Canadian trawlers, but by a much larger and more rapidly growing fleet of state-owned vessels operated under the flags of the U.S.S.R., Poland and East Germany.
In this connection, I should like to quote another study which we commissioned and whose results we have now received. It states:
Concern has been growing, particularly in the last decade, over the very large quantities of groundfish taken from the sea in the ICNAF area.
"ICNAF" stands for International Convention for Northwest Atlantic Fisheries. The report continues:
Biologists collecting and analyzing the data are warning the countries fishing in the area that the resource is fast reaching maximum sustainable yield. The warning is particularly strong for haddock and cod where maximum sustainable yields have been reached and in fact surpassed in some of the ICNAF sub-areas.
Indications are that haddock stocks are in a very poor state particularly in the southwestern portion of the Convention area. Though the cod catch could be expanded slightly in some sub-areas, the maximum sustainable yield seems to have been surpassed in 1968. All indications are that efforts by ICNAF member countries will continue to grow and that the area will be seriously overfished within a very few years.
These are the facts. All the world has the facts, really. The living resource out over our continental shelf areas is under heavy pressure. Some species are over-exploited already, yet foreign countries are stepping up their fishing pressure. As far as they are concerned there are no rules in this game. Certainly, there are no rules yet; it is a matter of first come, first served, and heaven help the hindmost.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Unfortunately the hindmost in this case is our own Canadian fishermen. They are being out-fished, not because they are less efficient, but because foreign governments are prepared to build massive fleets and run them like military operations. Our individual enterprisers, our rugged inshore fishermen, our small long-line operators and trawler operators-our God fearing, self-respecting fishermen-are no match for these gigantic adversaries. They are crushing us by the sheer weight of their tonnage and their gear, and

November 3, 1969
The Address-Mr. Davis our commercial fishing activity is being compressed into the smaller and less productive areas of the continental shelf. Our inshore fishermen are being hurt. Indeed, all Canadian fishermen are being hurt.
There has been a great deal of talk recently about the loss of marine life due to the sinking of the big oil tanker the Torrey Canyon off the south coast of England. Although this was a terrible thing, the damage to the marine ecology of that area brought about by the sinking of the Torrey Canyon was small compared to the havoc being wrought persistently year after year by some of the world's big, long distance fishing fleets. In a year they kill hundreds of times as many fish and other marine organisms as did the Torrey Canyon. They kill them every bit as effectively as hundreds of thousands of tons of oil did in that case. Equally important, they clean off the grounds in so far as future generations of fish and fishermen are concerned.
Fortunately the oil from the Torrey Canyon is disappearing. It is gradually evaporating or being oxidized in the sea itself. The same cannot be said of these giant fishing fleets which are growing in size and are taking more fish than ever before; and they are taking this fish without regard to sound conservation practice.
Worst of all for Canadians, these fleets are doing this just outside our own exclusive fishing zones and out over our own continental shelf. They are doing this to stocks of fish on which we have depended for centuries and on which we have every right to depend in the future.
We must bring this situation under control. We must press for the effective management of marine resources to the limit of our own continental shelf and beyond. This we must do at the next Law of the Sea Conference, and we must do it not only in the interests of our own inshore fisherman but in the interests of all mankind.
Hon. members will also have seen references in the Speech from the Throne to the need to provide good paying jobs to Canadians in those parts of the country which have been less fortunate than others.

speechtext:
From an income point of view, many of our fishing communities are on the bottom rung of the ladder. They need government help. They need help from their industry. More than anything else, our fishermen need useful occupations, jobs in the fishing industry that will pay well and offer a measure of security over the long run.
Fishermen in our inland waters have gained a greater measure of security and are receiving higher incomes as a result of our new Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, the legislation setting up which, hon. members will recall, was passed last spring. We plan during the coming session to set up a Salt Fish Development Agency with the same objectives in mind. Meanwhile, our new Department of Regional Economic Expansion is doing its utmost to round out our local fishing economies with a view to removing many of the financial inequalities of the past.
But what good will all these measures do if the resource itself is undermined? What good will all this legislation do if pollution is allowed to destroy our marine life, or if foreign fishing fleets continue to make it harder to catch fish? Obviously, we must deal with this much bigger problem of conservation and good management, and deal with it not only on a national scale but on a global scale as well.
We must take our case, if necessary, to the United Nations. Certainly, we must take it to the next Law of the Sea Conference, which hopefully will be in 1971. We must do our utmost to bring order out of chaos. The question is no longer that of unlimited freedom to fish; rather it is that of conservation in the best sense of the word, of protecting the resource from serious depletion and of putting all our fisheries, Canadian and international, on a sustained yield basis.
We must protect ourselves wherever necessary. Certainly, we must protect our fishermen and their families. But always there is the need for co-operation. As citizens of an affluent nation, we do not want to keep all of our material wealth to ourselves. We want to manage it well, but we are also prepared to share it with others. This is a note that I would like to strike with regard to the harvesting of our fishery resource both in Canada and out over our continental shelf. It is an approach which, I am sure, will command itself to developing nations everywhere.
November 3, 1969

As the Prime Minister said in the House of Commons the other day, as reported at page 39 of Hansard:
Part of the heritage of this country, a part that is of increasing importance and value to us, is the purity of our water, the freshness of our air, and the extent of our living resources. For ourselves and for the world we must jealously guard these benefits. To do so is not chauvinism, it is an act of sanity in an increasingly irresponsible world.
With this statement I agree. I agree with it not only in respect of our inland waters and Canada's exclusive fishing zones, but in respect of the continental shelf areas as well. I believe we should do our utmost to conserve these marine resources, to protect them and to harvest them with due regard not only for our fishermen today but for our future fishermen.
We do not ask that we have the exclusive right to fish anywhere. We do not ask for the exclusive right even to fish in our own continental shelf areas. But what we do ask is that others respect the same laws of nature and the same laws of economics as we; that they conduct themselves on the high seas in a manner that is consistent with the interests of all mankind.

Thank you again, Mr. Speaker. In view of the contribution just made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose), he should not be permitted to participate further in the debate.
This is the Throne Speech debate, so called. I listened to the Speech from the Throne and read it over a number of times. To me, it is an impossible item for debate. It does not invite debate, it defies it. I am not saying there is nothing in it or that it does not contain vague suggestions. What I am saying is that it is a catalogue, and I do not think we could debate it any more than we could debate the Ottawa telephone directory or the list of new books available at the Parliamentary Library.
I am sincere in saying that because appended to the Throne Speech is a list of almost six dozen pieces of legislation. There is no doubt that some good, solid legislation is contained in this list, but certainly no one can say that list provides us with anything that is debatable at this point. We are going to deal with the Small Business Loans Act amendment. We do not know if these loans are going to be increased, cut out, or what will happen. The 
list also indicates we will deal with an investment companies bill and the Expo winding-up bill. Apparently we will also deal with a young offenders bill. We have no details of these measures and do not know what is intended. In order to debate the Throne Speech as such, we will have to wait until some of these pieces of legislation are presented. However, this debate does give hon. members an opportunity to range rather widely in respect of a variety of subjects.
The first comment I should like to make is that the period set aside for the Throne Speech debate this year is just another example of the phasing out of Parliament. There is a pattern being set. A few days before the Throne Speech we heard a statement from the Prime Minister concerning how much he believed in, appreciated and respected this institution of Parliament. When we heard that we knew there was something coming.
The next thing we heard was that, for the first time in history, the hour for the delivery of the Throne Speech had been changed from three o'clock in the afternoon to ten o'clock in the morning. If that is not part of the downgrading process or phasing out of Parliament, then I do not know what I am talking about. When the Speech from the Throne is delivered at that time the function of Parliament is not the same since the speech does not receive the same attention as one delivered at the traditional hour of three o'clock in the afternoon. The next Speech from the Throne, which will probably be the last one, will likely be delivered at 7 a.m. or earlier.
The making of a president is taking place, and the president is not being made by anyone other than the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). This should be very obvious to all hon. members. I do not know whether that is good or bad as I have not thought much about it, but I think hon. members should be told what is taking place. That should be the obvious thing to do. Parliament should have some say as to its future. It should not be left to one man, or three men at the most, to phaseout what this country has cherished for so long.

I would like to explain the composition of my constituency. Many people seem to be under the impression that I represent only the city of St. Boniface, but my constituency comprises three large urban areas within the greater Winnipeg area. They are Transcona, a city of 22,000 people, city of St. Vital with a population of 30,000, and St. Boniface itself with a population of 48,000, plus two country points, lie des Chenes and St. Adolphe which are devoted to mixed farming. In fact, in the area of St. Adolphe farmers are still waiting to harvest their grain, since they have experienced very poor weather during the harvesting season.
The largely populated area that I represent encompasses a variety of ethnic groups, and these western Canadians represent a true example of understanding and unity in Canada.
Transcona is a fairly new city. It originated in 1912, and most of its labour force depends for work on the CNR shops located in that city. The residential city of St. Vital is the place from which Louis Riel came, and his home there will become an historical site with assistance from the local, provincial and federal levels of government.

The city of St. Boniface, founded in 1818, is often called the cradle of Christian civilization in western Canada. It is there that as early as 1800 most of our ancestors, the coureurs de bois, came to settle with Lord Selkirk. I regret that I cannot say more today about the history of St. Boniface.

I would like first to express my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address, the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) for their opening remarks. They spoke of the relevancy of parliament and I hope their colleagues will give special heed to their criticisms because it seems to this government that parliament has become a rather torturous exercise. We invariably get the impression they would like to scrap the whole institution. I would remind hon. members that when we speak in this chamber we are not only speaking to those in this House, but to all Canadians.
The opening speeches more or less set the tone for this debate. We have heard suggestions from subsequent speakers as to how government should function, and they ranged all the way from a dictatorship to a republic to a corporation with a board of directors. I do not intend to deal at length with the relevancy or irrelevancy of this institution. I simply want to say that, as far as I am concerned, it is a matter of one's own personal initiative and participation in carrying out the responsibilities which we accepted when we offered ourselves for this honoured position. Above all, it is the opportunity to serve Canada and to serve those who sent us here.
Referring directly to the Speech from the Throne, I may say I found it a rather generalized document containing very little to get excited about. There are, however, one or two matters to which I would like to refer and comment upon. There are some items in the speech of which I approve and there are

others, which I will deal with later, that have been omitted, either deliberately or unintentionally.

I wish to make it abundantly clear at the outset that I approve of this measure and I intend to support its passage in the House. No doubt some people in this country may question this legislation, but I ask them to bear in mind that we have reached a period where our younger generation is seeking greater responsibility. We hear the cry that our young are irresponsible, but how can they ever become responsible or take up the challenge of responsibility if they are not given the opportunity of meaningful participation?

We in the Province of Alberta have for some time allowed citizens aged 19 and over the privilege of voting, and the results have proved to be very satisfactory. I hope that in due course we may expect the institution of a uniform voting age across this country. I also hope parliament will consider the possibility of lowering the age at which young people may legally enter into contracts. It is somewhat ridiculous that a young person aged 18 can vote in a federal election, and influence the choice of a government, while being unable to enter into a contract to buy an automobile if he is self-sufficient, or self-supporting.
Since I became a member of this House my party has given me special responsibilities for dealing with youth matters and developing liaison between that segment of our society and our own caucus. I must say this has been one of the most gratifying duties I have had the privilege of undertaking since I took my seat in this honourable House. The association I have had, as a result, with our young people has convinced me that an enormous amount of energy and enthusiasm exist among our youth-enthusiasm for Canada. All we have to do is harness it.
Certainly, there are some radical differences of opinion, but this is natural in a free society. I would remind hon. members that radical differences of opinion prevail between senior members of our society, too. When any group, whether composed of the young or the old, feels a sense of alienation and frustration, it is bound to react. I am confident that the proposed legislation concerning the voting age could provide a foundation for sound, sensible involvement on the part of youth for the good of Canada. However, no one should expect that the mere passage of a bill will satisfy all the aspirations of Canada's youth. Not only
DEBATES	427
The address-Mr. Mazankowski should political parties give the youthful segment of society adequate opportunity to be heard, but immediate steps should be taken by all levels of government and by the public at large to encourage our young people to become actively involved in the activities of political parties; positive measures should be taken to encourage them to opt into our political society and work from within, rather than to opt out.
Above all, our educational facilities should begin to instil a little moral fibre, in place of the attempts to dissolve this moral fibre which now prevail. Programs of education should be geared to orientate and familiarize youth with the nature of our political framework at an early age so that voting becomes a meaningful privilege rather than a mere exercise.
I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his colleagues are not misled by an impression that because they have promised to introduce this particular measure they will necessarily have a monopoly of support from the young of Canada, and thus have provided the means of buying their way back to power. It may be that the right hon. gentleman's own party has failed in its dealings with youth. If I am correct, there is a fair amount of disillusion being felt among the young Liberal elements of his own party. I am sure it is fair to say that all political parties have considered lowering the voting age. I can certainly affirm that the subject has been actively considered, and the principle endorsed by the Progressive Conservative party.
As 1 have said, a simple lowering of the voting age will not satisfy all the aspirations of Canada's youth. Indeed, perhaps we are wrong when we think of today's unrest as being a "youth problem". It might be more helpful to consider this whole perplexing situation involving youth and society as being a "society problem" rather than a "youth problem". Have we earnestly tried to understand the young, or have we merely allowed them to live in their own sub-culture?
One of the most pressing problems facing society today concerns the use of drugs. I wish to emphasize what was said by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) when he suggested we should move very carefully and cautiously in considering legalization of the use of marijuana.
