The address-Mr. Mazankowski concerning certain types of drugs, and I hope these will be subjected to a comprehensive review. I have in mind particularly present laws as they relate to the use of such drugs as "speed" and heroin. The whole question of drug use is an exceedingly complex one. We must find means of analysing the state of mind of our young people who Eire taking drugs, and we must seek to understand why they are doing so. Meanwhile, until we are able to secure sufficient information as to the total implications of the use of marijuana, I submit we would be committing a grave error were we to move at this time in the direction of legalizing this drug. I believe that we, as legislators and as citizens, must take account of the growing use of drugs in our society. I would recommend that immediate steps be taken to familiarize the young, as well as others, with the dangers and implications of the use of all drugs. Specifically, I should like to make the following recommendations:
1.	That a system of centres be established across Canada to provide information, consultation and assistance on a more humane and rational basis to drug users. This organization should be federally funded.
2.	That further funds be made available for research into the effects and nature of drugs.
3.	That a national drug foundation be established for the administration of the previous two recommendations, for the co-ordination of research and for the exchange of information.
I might add that I intend to put forward a private member's bill dealing with this matter; I hope we shall have an opportunity to discuss it fully in this chamber. Until we have compiled a total assessment backed up by scientific and medical data, I submit we should move very cautiously. On the other hand, we should move vigorously in undertaking a comprehensive review and study of the state of mind of the young; above all, we must discover the underlying reason why so many become users of drugs.
We have heard a great deal recently about the Company of Young Canadians and its activities, and the controversies surrounding them. I personally believe that the majority of Canadians are fed up to the teeth with the CYC and I submit that the whole organization should be scrapped.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I realize that there may be some dedicated and sincere people within the organization of

the Company of Young Canadians, but these are in the minority and have the least influence. The organization seems to be dominated by a bunch of long haired, bearded radicals who do not believe in any established values, including the responsibility of having to work to eat. By virtue of its name and its past record, it implies that all youth in this country are radicals and subversives. I say that the damage this organization has done to the youth of Canada is irreparable, and we must abandon it before we turn all citizens of this country against our youth.
I suggest that if like the Canadian Union of Students, this organization had to operate on voluntary contributions and voluntary membership, it would collapse within 24 hours. Further, I should like to point out that the mere fact that the Canadian Union of Students has failed is ample proof that the majority of youth in Canada want no part of radicalism, subversion and mutinous activities.
Coming from an agricultural area I would be remiss if I overlooked some of the glaring problems facing western agriculture, as the government seems to have done in its Speech from the Throne. The Throne Speech contains one piece of proposed legislation to attempt to alleviate the desperate situation that exists in the west. I refer to the Canada Grain Act, which I suspect will merely lower prices to the producer while allowing greater market flexibility.
It is not my intention to go into depth with regard to the problems confronting agriculture. I am sure they are well known to all members of the house, including the Prime Minister who visited the west recently. These problems have been ably restated by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Southam) and the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Downey).
To sum up the situation briefly, let me simply say that conditions in this area have not improved one iota during the last 12 months. There has been a continual deterioration in the situation, with very little evidence of hope in sight. Quite frankly, the agricultural picture in the west is one of gloom. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but the whole rural community appears to be in jeopardy.
I become very confused when, on the one hand, the government classifies agriculture as expendable and plans for the early retirement of farmers, encourages these people to leave their farms and transfer to the cities, while, on the other hand, the Prime Minister suggests that rural life is worth preserving, as he
November 3, 1969	COMMONS
stated in his speech on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. Such statements are contradictory.
As far as I am concerned, rural life does have something to offer. It breeds self-reliance, self-discipline and self-determination. If this government were to take positive measures to stimulate rural life, then I would support them, as I am sure would many other members of the House.
I recall that the late General Eisenhower, who grew up in the small community of Abilene, Kansas, said that the robust life he had led as a prairie youngster, camping with friends, roughing it with his five brothers, helping to do the family chores, earning money on the side and learning the stern but compassionate rural ethic, were all part of the great and priceless heritage of living in a small town.
I should like to know why the Prime Minister, his colleagues and assistants, do not get together and face squarely the problem of rural life and agriculture. I believe it is high time they realized that agriculture is a necessary part of the Canadian economy, and that a vast number of Canadians prefer living in the country to urban life.
The production of food is more important today than ever before in world history. The Food and Agriculture Organization suggests that by 1975 a desperate shortage of food will exist in the world. This talk we hear about lack of markets and surplus of grain is sheer nonsense. The simple fact of the matter is that we are just not getting our share of the market. In 1966-67, we achieved 26.3 per cent of the world wheat market. In 1967-68 our percentage dropped to 17.2 per cent. Figures for the 1968-69 crop year are not yet published, but I suspect our percentage is even further below last year's, probably around 15 per cent.
We have not been selling our grain. I submit that what is required is a national grain selling agency with a progressive and imaginative policy. Such an organization should be organized in consultation with the producers. For too long have agricultural policies been formulated behind closed doors. We now have a new minister in charge of grain. With all due respect to the previous minister, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), who is a very amiable fellow, he knew as much about growing, marketing and selling wheat as I know about walking on the moon.

The Address-Mr. Mazankowski
In addition, we should introduce immediately a program to appraise and completely reassess our grain handling techniques and distribution methods. I think our methods of handling and distributing are outdated outmoded, and lack efficiency. It seems to me that our method of grain handling is the only part of the whole spectrum of grain production and marketing that has not changed one iota during the last 25 years. Certainly, the criterion we should aim at is to become more efficient and streamlined.
We all recall the election promise that if the Liberal party were elected to office in three years we could look for sales of one billion bushels of wheat. Half that time has passed and the only notable achievements in the grain marketing field so far have been lost sales. For a year and a half the government has been aware of the grain marketing problem. It has sent out surveyors and task forces and has established advisory councils. Even the Prime Minister was dispatched on a western tour. A grain council was set up, but I have heard nothing from it since its inception.
The government has suggested that farmers should diversify. I say, diversify to what? Beef? The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) has looked after that by proposing a boycott of beef. Beef prices are too high, and he maintains that the bulk of the increase is being passed on to the producer. Although diversification might solve some agricultural problems, it must be handled in a manner that is commensurate with the region. For example you cannot raise beef on the wheat plains of Saskatchewan. Therefore, a co-ordinated program of regional diversification in consultation with the provinces is required.
I believe it is the duty of the government accurately to analyse the supply and demand position of certain commodities and to encourage farmers to produce to meet those needs. However, no action of this kind has been taken by the government to cope with the situation and, above all, to meet the growing crisis.
At the present time farmers in the northern part of the prairies are undergoing difficulties resulting from adverse weather conditions. As the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) pointed out today, in many areas 90 per cent of the harvest still remains in the fields. I know the minister and his colleague, the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang), have visited the west and are analysing the situation. The province of Alberta has already announced its
November 3, 1969

The Address-Mr. Mazankowski intention to provide some form of assistance. But I submit this is a joint responsibility. I hope the minister will stand in his place and make an announcement this week in order to put the farmers at ease. The farmers are short not only of grain but of straw and feed to winter their livestock. So, certainly some assistance is necessary.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Some time ago Parliament was asked to approve and establish a department of regional expansion. We were led to believe this new program would benefit all Canadians suffering as a result of living in slow growth areas. We were led to believe that all areas suffering from regional disparity and drifting out of the mainstream of Canada's economic progress would be included. The fact is today that areas in Alberta and Western Canada which have experienced slow growth and have faced difficult times have been excluded. By an odd coincidence the only area of Alberta that appears to be in need of economic assistance, according to the minister and this new department, lies in the constituency represented by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson). It is this kind of thing that makes western Canadians skeptical of the good faith of this government.
If the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) were to take a completely unbiased look at the economic plight of Canada today, I believe he would decide to treat the whole Canadian agricultural area as a designated area for economic assistance. The great tragedy of this country is that hundreds of thousands of solid, taxpaying productive citizens are being driven from their preferred occupations by a combination of government indifference and lack of leadership. Canada's agricultural community is a valuable national asset, not only as a producer of food and of exports, but as a reinforcement for the framework of Canadian society.
I should like to comment briefly on the situation of our veterans and the Woods report. I do know that the Standing Committee on Veterans' Affairs has been meeting and considering this document. I simply want to go on record as supporting the recommendations in the Woods report. I speak on behalf of all those I represent and on behalf of the many members of the Legion in the area surrounding my constituency.

Let me particularly emphasize the need for an equitable basic rate of pension related to the rate for unskilled labour in the public service, as outlined in information given to the 1919 parliamentary committee. It seems to me grossly inequitable that there should be a discrepancy now between the basic pension and the rate for unskilled labour to the tune of approximately $1,000, particularly in this time of rampant inflation and rising living costs. The whole approach to the adjudication of claims must be put on a more humane and rational basis, emphasizing the application of the benefit of the doubt.
Having regard to the Legion magazine, I submit that equitable mailing rates should be re-established to allow the Legion magazine, Canada's voice of the veterans, to once again enjoy parity with some of the subversive publications which have been disseminating malicious propaganda. I am sure it is no secret to hon. members or the public that the Legion's publications were saddled with a whopping 1400 per cent increase in mailing rates. Certainly, there can be no justification for this.
In concluding my remarks, I should like to put in a plug for my good friends and neighbours of the city of Edmonton. As you may know, the city of Edmonton is known as the gateway to the north. It is Canada's only major city-as a matter of fact, it is Canada's fourth largest city-that does not enjoy a direct international air service link with the United States. You may be aware that the citizens of Edmonton are conducting a vigorous campaign in support of the request by North-West Orient Airlines for the right to link up Edmonton with Minneapolis, Chicago and Anchorage. I am sure I do not have to go into detail with regard to the economic advantages which this would have for the city of Edmonton and the province of Alberta. As a matter of fact, the future growth of Edmonton and Northern Alberta could very well be hindered if a favourable decision is not made.
An indication of the desire to have this service implemented is evidenced by the fact that more than 125,000 signatures, backed by more than 200 business enterprises, have been collected, together with written support in an accompanying brief which has been submitted to the chairman of the Air Transport Committee which will be reviewing these bilateral agreements this month. I want to go on record as being one of those actively engaged in supporting this application and I
November 3. 1969	COMMONS
urge those who are charged with the responsibility of making this decision to react in a favourable manner, thereby giving Edmonton the opportunity to enjoy similar service to that enjoyed by all other major cities in this country. If such service is not established, it will simply mean that Edmonton will be doomed to become a second class city in Canada.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members for your attention.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise in this famous chamber and be identified in some way with the many speeches that have been given during this rather lengthy debate on the Speech from the Throne. I want to identify myself with all members in this house who commended the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) on the very excellent speeches they made at the initiation of this debate.
At this time, I should like to say a few words about my own constituency and then deal with three different topics. As hon. members will have noted when Your Honour gave me the floor, my constituency is officially called Lanark and Renfrew. This is most unfortunate, not because it is called Lanark and Renfrew but because I represent three counties in Ontario, Lanark, Renfrew and Carleton. I have difficulty in convincing the people of Carleton that they are in fact included. For that reason, I have a private member's bill before this house asking that the name be changed to include Carleton.
I am also aware as we sit here day in and day out, week in and week out, to quote a famous member of this House, that "you cannot tell the depth of the well by the length of the handle on the pump", and that similarly you cannot always tell by the speeches made how great or bow small is the contribution.
The three topics I want to deal with in the few minutes my time will permit-and perhaps I cannot cover them all-are the initiation of full diplomatic relations between the government of Canada and the Vatican; the Canadian rural dilemma, and additional means whereby regional disparity can be significantly reduced. This may seem like a very large slice from the cake. Perhaps I will not get around to all three, but I want to share some of my convictions, thoughts and research on at least two of these topics.
DEBATES	431
The Address-Mr. McBride
My position regarding the recognition of the Vatican can be put very simply by saying I am not in support of it but rather strongly opposed to it. This may be surprising to some hon. members. They may suggest that, as a member on the government side of the House, I should support it. They may suggest I have some prejudices and so on. For my own satisfaction, and hopefully for the edification of the House, I will as lucidly and as briefly as I can indicate why I am not in favour of recognition of the Vatican in the sense of establishing full diplomatic relations. I have already indicated my feelings to the people of my constituency, to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp).
First, let me make one clarification. Some people say we are not establishing diplomatic relations with the Roman Catholic church but rather with the Vatican city state. It seems to me, if we analyse this situation for a moment, it is easy to see that diplomatic relations are not established between two sets of buildings; they are not established between pillars and they are not established between some kind of parliamentary assembly hall in nation A and some kind of assembly hall in nation B. Rather, they are established between governments, between those who, in fact, represent the people who live in those respective countries. It is between the government of Canada and the government of Vatican city that diplomatic relations have been established. Who is the government of Vatican city? Well, Pope Paul VI and the Curia happen to be the government of Vatican City. Who are they? They are none other than the titular and actual heads of the Roman Catholic church. In elementary school, I believe it was, we learned a mathematical principle that things equal to the same thing are equal to each other. So, it seems to me in a very real sense that we are like the Irish Rovers and their Unicorn when we say we are not involved with the Roman Catholic church but are just establishing diplomatic relations with the Vatican. We are playing silly games.
[DOT] (4.20 p.m.)
If the Pope is not the head of the Roman Catholic church, then I do not know who is and neither does anyone else. So, let us dispel once and for all the idea that they are not one and the same thing. I repeat that our diplomatic relations were not established with a group of buildings but with the government of the Vatican. That government is the Holy See of Rome and the Holy See of Rome is the
November 3, 1969

The Address-Mr. McBride primary bishopric of the Catholic church in the world. I say all of this to lay the foundation for hon. members in this chamber who may be interested in, or will at least tolerate, the presentation I am about to make. I must say this to clarify the reason for my opposition to the move to recognize the Vatican.
The recognition of the Vatican by Canada is not something that can simply be identified with or even compared with the 68 other countries which have established diplomatic relations with the Vatican before us. The reason we in Canada cannot compare our own situation with the situations which have existed in all the other countries is simply that we have a history that is distinctly and uniquely unlike the history of any one of those other 68 countries. It is basically different in relation to this topic.
What, in fact, does our history have to do with our establishing diplomatic relations with the Vatican now? Well, fellow members of this House, I am desperately convinced it has a great deal to do with it. It has a great deal to do with whether or not we should have diplomatic relations. I regret that the historic facts have received so little, almost pathetically little, consideration in the discussion or in public debate of this subject. Therefore, I beg hon. members to allow me to sketch for a few moments some of the brief and pertinent facts of the past out of which this nation's present has come and which bear directly on our diplomatic relations with the Vatican. Let us all remember-and this is almost a cliche or obvious truism-that we do not exist in a vacuum. We all have a history; we have come from somewhere, we are going to somewhere and where we have been has a great influence on where we are now and where we shall be later.
In order to make my point extremely clear I must go back some 712 years. In the year 1257-

I have done my research. In the year 1257, the Sorbonne was founded in France. From the time of the establishment of the Sorbonne, the Roman Catholic church in France was always much influenced by a teaching that could most simply be described in this way. The Roman Catholic church in France-this belief existed there to a greater extent than in any other country-should be more or less free from the authority of the Pope and should be a nationally autonomous

church. That idea has since that early date been of great influence in France. The Church should be nationally autonomous to the extent that even the appointment of the bishops should either be done by the king or the king should have the last say in the appointment thereof, rather than the Pope. This form of Catholicism quite naturally, came to be known in historical circles as Gallicanism French Catholicism has always been extremely Gallican. The other extreme, the opposite to Gallicanism, is where you are directly under the Papacy; where the bishops in another country-not merely in Vatican city or in Italy but in any country of the world- are appointed directly by the Pope. This is called ultramontanism.
I do not wish to appear to be a teacher or in any sense to be talking down to members, but this whole debate in respect of diplomatic relations with the Vatican has been entirely too shallow. It has ignored our history and has failed to note that Gallicanism was the Catholicism that came to Canada when the French settlers from France first arrived here. This was Gallican Catholicism which meant that the bishops were appointed by the king, to put it in its simplest form. When New France was settled, the religion was Catholicism and it was Gallican Catholicism. All of the leaders of the Catholic church in New France had very strong Gallican sympathies. We all know the history, but I must set the stage for what I am attempting to establish here. New France eventually fell to the abhorred British. It was very obvious, as in all cases where the British were able to conquer some other colonial power, that they had to give rights and privileges to the residents of New France. These had to be extended by the British or they could not hope to retain control over their freshly acquired territory.
If one studies British colonial expansion, one will find that this happened all over. The fact that the French court of the day-sort of back home on the ranch in France-had fallen on evil days meant that New France was reduced to the level of an abandoned orphan. It was left in the arms of the loathsome British. All of this has nothing to do with what I or other members think; this is the history of our country. This meant that the leaders of New France approached the British and said that one of the things they wanted was religious freedom; freedom to pursue the religion they had known. The British said they would grant religious freedom but that appointment of bishops by the
November 3, 1969

King of France would absolutely not be allowed and that there was no way the King of France was going to meddle in the affairs of New France any longer. So this, for the Gallican catholics of New France was a difficult situation. The leaders came back with a counter-proposal. The counterproposal was that if they could not continue to have the bishop appointed by the King of France, they would like to go directly to the Pope and become ultramontanistic. The British, who wanted to get free of French political and practical involvement in North America, said fine. So, something happened in Canada that was absolutely unique in the world.
Overnight, these people, who had been strongly Gallican, became members of one of the world's most ultramontanistic churches. This is the point in North America when the interests of the French speaking people and the interests of the Pope of Rome become fused into one. From then on, the two were linked together. This is a fact of history and this is a situation which does not exist in any other country. It may be that French speaking members from Quebec in this assembly would Stand up and say I am talking about things which are just ancient history and which are not relevant any more in French Canada. They might say that the opinions of French Canadians and the Pope are not one and the same any longer. But this conviction has not been understood in English speaking Canada or in areas where the population is non-Catholic and English-speaking. I have always found in Ontario and in western Canada there is a distinct conviction that this is the situation; that the historical fusion of French rights and the interests of the Papacy are still one and the same.
[DOT] (4.30 p.m.)
One year ago a very special bill known as the languages bill was introduced in this house. It was my conviction that it was a fantastically good bill, and I supported it unreservedly. As a result, and because of the history of Canada, I went into my constituency and said to my people: I know that so far as you English-speaking Canadians are concerned you still believe that the interests of the French language Canadians and the Pope of Rome are one and the same. But that is not so, I said. This was a coincidence of history but it is dead. It will not be perpetuated. They are two separate things. This government is interested in extending French language rights. We are not interested in the Roman Catholic church one way or the other.

The Address-Mr. McBride I made a very fine case. I think hon. members can see where I am going because when we established diplomatic relations with the Vatican, people like myself, from English speaking constituencies, who believe in Canada and who believe we should have an extension of the French language rights in Canada, had the rug pulled right out from under our feet.
I am embarrassed to say that not only has my credibility been damaged but the credibility of the government in which I have a minute share as a backbencher has also been damaged because if this type of action is going to undermine our progress toward bilingualism and resurrect the corpse that I had told people was laid to rest for ever-and I believed that that was the case-then this is a sad, sad day. I want to make my position very clear. Judging from what an hon. member to my right is saying under his breath, I am getting it across. I want to make it clear that I do not support this government action. It is most unfortunate that we have perpetuated what I had hoped was over and done with for ever. Religion and language should be two separate things. If there is anything that can be done to help Englishspeaking Canadians to recognize that we are not in any way perpetuating Catholicism, either pushing it up or down, but that language is one thing and religion is another, I would still like to hear about it and be a part of it.
My case has tumbled to the ground. For that, I am embarrassed and sad. I make my position clear and say that this has been a most unfortunate thing. It is a heavy price to pay at home to have millions of Canadians, who are in fact not Catholic and who speak English, believe that this government which is for extending the rights of French Canada is ipso facto and automatically for extending the rights of the Roman Catholic church in precedence over all others. This is very sad. However, that is water under the bridge and there is nothing I can do but cry the blues.
I do not want to use up too much of my time on this subject since there is a second point I would like to make. I will concentrate on one small area of the globe, namely Latin America, an area that holds my interest very strongly. There are 22 countries in Latin America and 20 of the 22 are predominantly Catholic. Of those 20, 19 are nations which have been colonized by either Spain or Portugal. The national churches in both those countries are Roman Catholic. The churches in both Spain and Portugal, if you know anything about the present day history, tend to
November 3, 1969

The Address-Mr. McBride be the most traditionally bound and tend to have the least ability of any national Catholic church in the world, in the context of their homeland, to manifest any relevent social conscience. In short, the missionaries who have gone out, as well as the whole of the churches in the 19 countries of Latin America, take their predominant tone and theme from Spain and Portugal. Therefore, in Latin America, the church has come to be too much identified with the establishment, with the people who have the power. As far as the mass of the people throughout Latin America are concerned, the people who have the power have the land, suppress the people, and have made a comfortable alliance with hunger, poverty, disease and illiteracy.
In increasing our own ties with the Vatican, we are identified with the establishment in a huge portion of the world where I, for one, want us to be future-oriented and identified with the mass of the people. In this sense, if you look into the future, the establishment of a diplomatic post at the Vatican is a disadvantage. Unfortunately, my time is running out and I will not be able to go into the other reasons. I have talked to other hon. members privately, and they have said they have never heard other people talking about these problems in discussing our relations with the Vatican. I am not attempting to suggest to the House that I have an insight which no other member has, but I thought these factors should be put on the record to indicate there are good reasons why it was a bad thing for Canada to establish diplomatic relations with the Vatican. Unfortunately, we are now on the side of yesterday. We are not standing with tomorrow. Too frequently, we creep where we should have walked and we walk when we should have run, but in this instance we ran forward only to catch up to yesterday.
I believe that bilingualism and bicultural-ism are more important than most of us think and that anything we do to diminish their importance is a step in the wrong direction. Therefore, I oppose the establishment of diplomatic relations with the Vatican.
Leaving that topic completely, I want to address myself for a few minutes before my time elapses to the problems in the Ottawa Valley and in my constituency, an area where roads are desperately inadequate, where avenues that will permit industry to place its products on the markets of Canada or of the world are so limited that industry is having a tough time in competing. We are in an area

that is not one of the designated areas in the regional development plan. For that reason, you will see on the order paper a notice of motion in my name that we should become a designated area. I hope it will be debated on some future occasion. We have some industry in our area, but the Ottawa Valley is primarily an agricultural area in a day when 7 per cent of our population is made up of farmers but when we are moving very swiftly to identify with the United States situation where less than 2 per cent of the population is in fact involved in primary production.
The problem in agriculture in Canada is a very simple one and I am familiar with it from first hand experience and professional training. In Canadian agriculture, the whole problem can be stated in one word-over production. In Ontario, we most certainly need- and I am not so familiar with the rest of Canada although I had the privilege of being a member of the Agriculture Committee as we travelled across the country-to control and organize our marketing. To do so, and to control our production, good supply management is essential. It is nowhere more essential than within the agricultural industry. In the midst of any attempt toward supply management, and any attempt to uproot or relocate people, no houses and much pollution, and we paramount. People-values cannot simply be thrown to one side. In Canada, we have a queer situation. We have cities with many people, no houses and much pollution, and we have rural areas with many houses, no pollution and no people. We need to balance these situations somehow or other. We need to get a little optimism in the pessimists and pessimism in the optimists.
To cope with this problem I have an idea, which may be farfetched but which I think ought to be given serious consideration. I call it the central agency for transportation, or, for short, CAT. The whole point of CAT, as I envisage it, would be that every manufacturer in the whole of Canada would pay no transportation costs to truckers or rail lines etc. Instead, all would pay an equalized levy to the central agency for transportation. CAT would levy an equal rate per ton or per hundredweight for transportation costs on all companies, whether they had to ship their goods 500 miles or two miles in every part of Canada. Thus, one of the most severe restrictions on decentralization of industry would be eliminated. It seems to me that although the regional incentives idea is a good one, it will never really work. We will never really achieve what we must achieve in Canada

unless some such additional scheme is adopted.

I know that many of the companies in the Ottawa valley area, which I represent, and companies in northern Ontario and elsewhere say, "Our problem is transportation costs. We have to compete with companies that are located only one mile away from those who buy their commodities." I would, therefore, leave the idea with the House that perhaps the Standing Committee on Transportation or the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) could consider some sort of central agency for transportation, an agency which would equalize transportation costs for all industries regardless of where they were located. Mr. Speaker, on rising to participate in the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne in this second session, I suppose it is normal and courteous to congratulate not only the two members who moved and seconded the Address in Reply to Her Majesty's representative but also to congratulate you, Sir, on having weathered the first term of this parliament, and all the officers who assist you in your work in this House, because it is only through the proper conduct of your duties that we are able to carry on in an effective manner on behalf of the people whom we represent.
The Address-Mr. D. MacDonald
Like so many other comments that have been made over the past few days, mine will be in nature a pot-pourri in an attempt to deal with some of the concerns that strike me as being important. One is tempted to respond to some comments that were made earlier, but I will refrain from doing that. Rather, I will deal with matters that I think are of very important concern, both to this House and to the country.
One of the chief concerns that people have had over the last year since the government took office-in fact, it is well over a year ago-has been the attempt to understand the shape and direction of its leadership. The shortest description that has been used up to now of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been that of a pragmatist. It is a very popular thing in the era of the 1960's to be regarded as a pragmatist. John F. Kennedy, who opened his leadership in this decade, was regarded as being a pragmatist above all else. In most quarters it is regarded as a compliment.
However, I would suggest that as the shape of the leadership of the government is becoming clear to us we are becoming more and more aware of the fact that it is led not by a pragmatist but by a legalist. For people in the future to understand the kind of decisions being taken, it will be important for them to understand the kind of leadership given. I would like to illustrate my suggestion that the Prime Minister is a legalist and practices a new kind of political philosophy that can be described as 'legalism' by giving three examples of three issues considered important to the people of Canada within the past year.
The first was one in which I was very closely involved-the whole business of the Nigeria-Biafra conflict, stretching over many months. There was great public agony, not only in this country but in many western countries, over the senseless slaughter taking place in the country formerly known as Nigeria and now known as Nigeria and Biafra. As recently as this month, one national church publication lamented in the strongest tones the inability of governments like our own to respond to the senseless loss of 2 million lives in little more than a year in that part of Africa. Our government has not acted. If we were to go through the various ins and outs of the discussions which have been held, and the things the government has said, and the attempts it has made to deal with this problem, one thing would become clear, that is that the government, from the beginning of

November 3, 1969

The Address-Mr. D. MacDonald its awareness of this problem, has been circumscribed by legalism.
Of course, a man of law such as our Prime Minister, and such as others who work with him, would quite naturally respond, "That is how we carry on our affairs, particularly those that pre-occupy the business of nations with nations." Mr. Speaker, I would say to you that when we very easily suggest that there is an accepted body of doctrine known as international law by which we can govern ourselves, then we have made the first basic mistake in trying to understand and deal realistically with what is happening in the international community.
We know only too well how ineffective the World Court at the Hague has been in trying to make its decisions stick, and this in fact in dealing with basic questions of international law. The international community is not one governed primarily by law and order. Rather, it is a human jungle. I suggest we have yet to reach that point where we can govern ourselves according to any kind of laid-down international dictum to which all nations, big and small, give assent. We know only too well that spheres of influence and powerful concerns play a much more important part in the decisions that are taken by governments than any adherence to some kind of abstract international law. Would to God that some kind of international law did, in fact, exist.
From the beginning, the Prime Minister has stated both publicly and privately that he could not act because it would be in contravention of international law. However, lawyers both in this country and in other countries who have spent some little time in examining the various international laws, so-called, that might apply to this kind of situation, and the various examples that could be culled from earlier decisions respecting international intervention, have argued strenuously that there is a good body of international law that would allow for a variety of creative responses to this situation. But we have not seen one ounce of solid, creative response to this most difficult problem. All we have heard from the beginning to the end has been a kind of resort to what I would call illustrations that bear no similarity to the problem, and these sometimes so crudely put as to be offensive.
Even more recently, we learned that our problems with regard to our sovereignty in the northern part of this country were placed in a great state of confusion because some months ago the Prime Minister suggested it was not at all clear what kind of jurisdiction

we would exercise in the waters between the islands in the Canadian Arctic archipelago. However, it is interesting that each time he has spoken since then he has moved back more and more to the position which has always been assumed by prime ministers in this country, the position that we do in fact claim sovereignty over all the waters that lie around the islands in the northern part of our country.
Now, the Prime Minister resorts to what to me seems the most strange way to get around this problem. Now, we are told that because of the danger of pollution, and because of the fact that the Eskimos for years have been walking on the ice as well as the land, we of course have jurisdiction and sovereignty in that part of the country. But naturally the Prime Minister will not speak forcefully until he has established, by some legal means that he has yet to make clear to us that he can proclaim and have it readily accepted internationally, that we are sovereign in that part of our country.
Thirdly, and perhaps of most immediate concern to people in our own land, there is the problem of inflation. Of course, inflation is a difficult problem to deal with, and to suggest it could be dealt with quickly or easily would be to ignore the real problems inherent in the situation itself. The government decided to establish a Prices and Incomes Commission which would attempt to determine what might be a reasonable increase for those asking for higher wages as well as for those who are asking for higher prices. Almost within a week of one another, we had two examples of the recommendations of that commission being ignored. The Canadian Labour Congress as much as said it was not prepared to co-operate with the commission, and one of our major steel companies announced that it was increasing the price of basic steel by 6 per cent. Today I hear that another firm has followed suit, with price increases of between 5J and 6 per cent. Of course, the Prime Minister has argued that the government does not want to interfere with the work of the Prices and Incomes Commission, because this is the commission's responsibility. Why the government feels this way is an intriguing question.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
When asked what action the government might take, because there seemed to be some doubt in the minds of some that the government might want to take action, the Prime Minister said that the question was being
November 3, 1969	COMMONS DEBATES	437
looked into. When he was asked if the federal government is empowered by the constitution to control prices and wages without encroaching upon certain powers he replied, as reported at page 235 of Hansard as follows:
This general matter has been referred for consideration to the Department of Justice which, as the hon. member knows, acts as an adviser to the government on constitutional and legal matters.
Have we reached that stage when the government of this country, on being asked a question affecting our basic economy, must refer the subject matter of the question to some legal tribunal in order that we may decide what right the government has to act? I wonder whether we have a government at all, or if we have not been ruled by some new kind of law society which will pass judgment from time to time on questions of the day that are of most legal interest. Mr. Speaker, the government this Prime Minister heads is not one of pragmatism but of legalism.

I feel it is unfortunate that the country will have to bear, for at least another three years, with this kind of legalistic behaviour.
As one looks at the realm of international affairs, one can see that in the dying years of the 1960's such behaviour did little to enhance Canada's image. We are told in the Speech from the Throne that we shall be intensifying our direct contacts with many of the governments and peoples of Latin America, Africa and Asia. Presumably, we intensify our contacts by closing up shop in various places in order that we can cut our expenditures or losses-choose your own term. Is this the way that we are to co-operate more closely with some countries and understand them more fully? At the time, we have pledged ourselves to be an active member of the United Nations, and we suggest that we are now in a position perhaps to play our part in revitalizing and strengthening the United Nations. I wonder if anyone in New York city, say, would, take such a statement seriously, especially if he realizes that in the last few years in major matters which have come to the forefront of international affairs, Canada has displayed no leadership in terms of insight or courage. We have been happy to pander to the ideas of many other countries, many of which are not great powers but small powers, when they have told us that our price for being accepted by the international group is for us to go along with other people's ideas.
The Address-Mr. D. MacDonald
It strikes me that we are verging on hypocrisy, Mr. Speaker, when we announce to the world that we are to establish, all on our own, an international development research centre. Sometimes I think that we see reflected in the makeup of this government the worst trends of Canadians who travel abroad. They have a smugness about them as they look at the difficulties from which our great neighbour, the United States, is trying to extricate itself, implying at the same time that although Canada is not so powerful we are really much better off and much better fellows. We can set up an international development research centre all by ourselves. Frankly, I do not know what we shall research. We have not even given the aid we have committed ourselves to give. I remember the figure of 1 per cent of our gross national product being mentioned in the grandiose pronouncements of our former prime minister a few short years ago.
In the Speech from the Throne, and in the Prime Minister's remarks, we see comments about the nature of our society, about its uncertainty, its shifting values and its propensity to action through violence. Some of that violence we have seen at close range. We are all genuinely concerned in this House about the ways in which traditional values and patterns of behaviour have undoubtedly changed. We are very much concerned that institutions such as this will not respond quickly enough, in terms of temperament and change, to the social realities of the country and of the world. But I say to you, sir, that as one reads the Speech from the Throne and the Prime Minister's remarks one will see little evidence that there is an awareness of what must be done, because the situation of today in the world has changed from that of only a few short years ago. If the Prime Minister and the government believe that all they have to do in the face of current unrest is lower the voting age by three years, then I say that he and the government have lost all sense of what it means to lead the country today. What use are all these public discussions and white papers, if the Prime Minister has decided that he will not listen to the recommendations of parliamentary committees and that the government will, so to speak, do its own thing? I say that he has not really committed himself to discover what is happening in this country today. It is interesting to note that while the Prime Minister, during his election campaign, spent some little time talking about the need for people to participate in government and about the
438	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. D. MacDonald need for them to communicate with him their concern about what is happening today, we see evidence that the government today is trying to dampen down discussion, avoid criticism and, in a sense, go its own sweet way.
No Canadian was more shocked than I was when hearing what the Prime Minister had to say about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Even more shocking was the lack of public outcry which ought to have arisen from what he said. It is hard to believe that only a few short years ago one Prime Minister was publicly rebuked for sending a personal letter to the president of the CBC; yet here we have another Prime Minister saying that if the CBC does not behave he will close down part of its network, and there is no outcry. Government interference in this field will mean that instead of public broadcasting in this country, something which is extremely valuable for the freedom of people, we shall have state broadcasting, which very few here seem to understand. It is interesting to note that France is in the process of moving away from state broadcasting and is going to public broadcasting.
On the other hand, under the direction of our Prime Minister, we are moving in the other direction. I hope that this serious folly on the part of the Prime Minister, occasioned perhaps by his desire to present some kind of heartwarming speech to his followers in Quebec, will be seriously reconsidered and that no more of these outbursts will be allowed to occur. I do not know how many such attacks it would take by a leader of a country upon its crown corporation before the corporation would crumble not only from within but from without. The Prime Minister has a rather unfortunate habit of talking against those who use rather aggressive ways of dealing with situations and then doing the same thing himself. He referred to the difficult situation that exists in Quebec, but not in terms helpful to the situation. There was a rather strange situation last week. In Montreal the Prime Minister made a speech which had great appeal to those in English speaking Canada who are looking for very simple answers to very complex problems. Following this, the leader of the Liberal Party in Quebec suggested exactly the opposite. If anyone understands whether there is some strange bond between the federal and the provincial branches of the Liberal Party in Quebec, I hope he will explain it to me because I have difficulty trying to consolidate this point of view into any kind of unanimity.

Much of what the Prime Minister has said about participation and the chance for involvement is a thin veneer with little reality behind it. He has been in his position for some months now. If he is serious about participation, beyond having a few more teenagers going to the ballot-box once every four years, it is time he proved it. There are some basic things the Prime Minister could do. I cannot understand why at the beginning of his leadership he did not seriously and publicly advocate the broadcasting of the sittings of this House and its committees so that all Canadians could be aware of what is happening in the forum that, hopefully, represents their national interests. I cannot understand why in this day and age, when we put so much emphasis on what we learn via radio and television, political leaders should be allowed to avoid facing the responsibility of broadcasting the proceedings of this House. I have not heard any good arguments against the same access being made available to the audio and visual media as is now available to the printed media, and has been for many years.
If there is any seriousness on the part of the government to at least expose this institution. and its committees to the country, and vice versa, surely broadcasting of our proceedings is a first requirement. Even that would be only a first step toward a major involvement of the Canadian people. If the government is concerned about the amount of antipathy and even cynicism that exists in the political processes of this country, confrontation of the kind the Prime Minister exhibits from time to time is really not the answer. It is sad that somebody who is reasonably bright should resort to what is not a
November 3, 1969
very bright technique in place of real political leadership. We must make changes in our institutions. Some of them must undergo major change if they are to work effectively for the remainder of this century. It is not enough to cling to the past or tinker with what I call incidentals; we must go to the bottom of basic problems. If we are not willing to consider these basic problems they will one day be forced upon us in a very unpleasant way.
We should not fool ourselves. Simply because we have elections from time to time and people seem reasonably satisfied with the leaders and representatives they elect does not mean that all is well. We know it is not. We know that times have changed greatly. People no longer want to be simply spectators in their own country. They want not only representation but genuine participation. They do not want a sham kind of participation that simply means they have been allowed to take part but their opinions are not worth very much. This is sometimes the way parliamentarians on committees feel when reports are made and they find the government has neither considered them important nor even considered them at all.
I hope we might get beyond some of the peripheral questions that seem to concern the government at the moment, and raise basic questions about how parliamentary democracy flourishes in the 'kind of technological age in which we live. We have acknowledged that new realities exist in our system, whether they be of communication, education, transportation or social interaction. Unless we are prepared to recognize this fact, the difficulties we have been experiencing will become greater and not less. It is my hope that in this session of Parliament, perhaps through a special committee or an effort by some members, we will begin to work on this question in a way that will allow the kind of genuine participation that Canadians not only ask for but require. If we do that we will have taken a genuine step toward the kind of participatory democracy that has too often been a slogan and seldom a fact.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we seem to be reversing the usual order today. In the last hour or two we have heard two clergymen in succession, followed by two farmers. This seems to be almost going from the sublime to the ridiculous.

speechtext:
I appreciate the opportunity to take part in this Throne Speech debate. I join those who have preceded me in congratulating the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) on their fine speeches when moving and seconding the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne last October 23.
Last year, on September 23, 1968, I spoke of the startling drop in farm income, especially in the prairies, which was experienced in the crop year 1967-68. The value of our wheat and wheat flour exports that year dropped to less than $700 million, after we had experienced the four best years in history when under a liberal government from 1963 to 1967 the value of our wheat and wheat flour exports averaged over $1 billion per year.
The downward trend continues. I have not seen exact figures, but we did export 305.8 million bushels of wheat in 1968-69. Calculated at $1.90 per bushel, which is probably high when one considers the low grade of some of that wheat, the export value for 1968-69 would amount to $581 million. Coupled with the drop in Wheat Board final payments last spring, the grain farmer's loss of income has reached the proportions of a national calamity. Let me assure the government, which is rightly concerned about inflation, that the prairie grain farmers are certainly not contributing to that problem; on the contrary, they are among those being victimized by it. I will have more to say about inflation later.
The fact is that we already have a full-fledged depression in the grain growing areas of the prairies which is affecting not only the farmers but those urban communities which
[The Deputy Speaker.]
DEBATES	November 3, 1969
exist mainly to serve the needs of the farmers. Many of these urban communities are rapidly becoming ghost towns.
Regional development was mentioned in the Throne Speech. I am happy to learn that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and in particular its incentive activities, will continue to get increased attention and funds. I was very pleased to learn that a large part of southern Saskatchewan has been made eligible for area development assistance. I welcome encouragement for industrial development and I know that we in southern Saskatchewan will do our best to make use of the help offered.
In this connection I was interested in a comment made earlier in the debate by the hon. member for York-North (Mr. Danson) which points up the contrasts in Canada. He said, as reported on page 108 of Hansard:
We are blessed in our region. We have expansion going on daily that would create headlines anywhere else. This hardly ruffles the surface. It is almost routine. I have in mind a 4,000 man increase in employment in one aircraft plant, of which most people in the area are not even aware, which puts additional pressure on the economy of our region. There was a $32 million development in one corner of my riding which I read about in the local suburban newspaper. So we enjoy success and prosperity beyond measure.
Things like that rarely happen anywhere in Saskatchewan. If they did, and especially if they should happen in my constituency, everybody would talk about it for years before and probably for years after. This contrast lends urgency to the development of the area incentives plan. However, I believe that positive action to improve the lot of the grain farmer would do more to quickly revive our ailing economy and put life back into the service industries on the prairies, on a shortterm basis at least.
May I again suggest that the government support the price of wheat at $1.95J as was done between August 1, 1967, and July 1, 1968. That was during the period when no International Grains Arrangement was in effect. Now that the IGA has been agreed to and ratified by the government, there is even more justification for the government supporting that minimum price. This is a government agreement, negotiated by governments, signed and ratified by governments, which has been broken by government action in the first year of a three-year term. Farmers planned their production and financing on the basis of that three-year agreement. Now suddenly they are left high and dry and are being made the victims of an international
November 3, 1969
price war between governments. No government would dare treat big industry or labour unions in such a cavalier fashion. So I renew my request that the government consider what farmers believe to be a legitimate claim for this kind of assistance.
Farmers appreciate the beginnings of a two-price system. The principle has been established. I call on the government to make it more realistic in terms of general price levels in the Canadian economy. I ask the government to provide some meaningful assistance to grain farmers who may wish to diversify, which is what some government spokesmen are recommending.
Much has been said in the last year or two about who was responsible for encouraging farmers to increase their grain production. At one of the many meetings I attended in my constituency this fall, one farmer, who must have had a good filing system or at least a better one than I have on the farm, produced a copy of "Farm Letter", which is a monthly publication of the federal Department of Agriculture. It contained an article entitled "Outlook 67" and was dated January 1967. It was issued with the authority of Hon. J. J. Greene, the then Minister of Agriculture. Let me read two short paragraphs on the outlook for wheat:
The forecast is for a carryover of 580 million bushels on July 31 when the crop year ends, and the experts say this is not too much.
Remember, they are referring to July 31, 1967, just a little over two years ago. Listen to this:
Continuing high production of wheat will be needed. But given average yields, Canada should be able to meet the demand by planting 30 million acres to wheat, the same as in 1966.
Can anyone deny at least some government responsibility for the wheat surplus?
In March of 1968, a little more than a year after that "Farm Letter" was published, the task force on agriculture said that farmers should progressively reduce their wheat acreage from 30 million to 20 million by 1980. There has been talk about supply management in this House. Grain farmers operate under the most stringent system of supply management one could possibly devise. I refer to the quota system, which in effect only allows us to deliver from the farms that which is actually sold. The quota system and the resulting pileup of surplus grain on the farms caused farmers to go halfway toward the suggested 12-year reduction of 10 million acres in one short season. Wheat acreage was cut almost 5 million acres in 1969. If farmers should continue at that rate-which is quite impossible, of course-we would reduce our
The Address-Mr. A. B. Douglas acreage to 20 million acres in two years instead of twelve. If carried further to an absurd conclusion, by 1974 we would seed no wheat at all.
The unpredictability of the wheat industry is demonstrated by the production this year: while the acreage went down by about 15 per cent, the production of wheat increased by over 4 per cent. Someone will say that farmers just used more fertilizer on the reduced acreage. I have in mind the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle). The use of fertilizer was almost cut in half in 1969, compared with 1968. The average yield increase from 22.1 bushels per acre to 27.2 bushels was almost entirely due to rain coming at the right time, and despite a reduction in the use of fertilizer.
The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Harries) made a very good point when he spoke in this debate last Thursday-I hope interested persons will take heed of what he said-as reported in Hansard for October 30, near the end of page 295 and on page 296. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I believe the word "not" was left out of the seventh line in the first column on page 296. I quote with approval one paragraph from page 296 of the hon. member's speech:
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I do not think it makes sense, Mr. Speaker, to permit Canadian agriculture to function on an external basis when virtually all the rest of the economy is functioning on an internal basis. This creates poverty and, in my view, conditions quite out of sympathy with, and inappropriate to, the kind of productivity that we can enjoy in Canada.
I urge the government to allow the budget to expand for agriculture rather than be constricted. Farmers are among those people referred to as being unable to exact from our economy their fair share of price and income increases. I believe that the people of Canada, who are on the average very prosperous, should through the federal government come to the aid of disadvantaged people such as the farmer, the fisherman, the pensioner and the slum-dweller.
Someone may ask, "Where can we get the money?" Again I refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona who I believe is a former dean of economics of the university at Edmonton. He suggested that crown corporations which have been successfully developed should be sold and the money used for other development. I would prefer that we dispose of other government agencies, particularly those that incur deficits. The first one that comes to mind is the Canadian

November 3, 1969

The Address-Mr. A. B. Douglas Broadcasting Corporation, which is expected to have a deficit of $151 million this year. I selected the CBC for more than financial reasons. They seem to be responsible to no one. I have not watched any CBC plays for years. I used to watch them but I could not stomach them. From my correspondence it seems that many people now have the same reaction. I am sure that few people would willingly pay to see some of the stuff the CBC puts out.
Most people in my area prefer the private network where management depends on public approval to make the operation pay. There is one exception. The private network station in Regina does not carry school television broadcasts. Early this fall the CBC unceremoniously switched stations in Regina with the private network, with the result that many schools which had purchased TV equipment and developed timetables making use of these broadcasts were left without the programs. One would think the CBC would have had enough consideration for its patrons to make arrangements with the other outlet to continue the service. The Don Messer fiasco was another example of the indifference of the CBC to its public. The CBC network and facilities should be worth a lot of money. We should sell the assets, use the money for more urgent programs and release almost $200 million a year of our annual budget for better uses.
I think funds could be diverted to greater advantage in the Department of Agriculture. My favourite suggestion is to dispose of the Tobacco Research Station at Delhi, Ontario, to the tobacco companies and save several hundred thousand dollars per year. It is ludicrous, in my opinion, to have on the one hand the Department of Health and Welfare spending large sums of money to combat the bad effects of the use of tobacco, while on the other hand the Department of Agriculture is spending large amounts to assist its production. There is also the question of the experimental station for fur-bearing animals which is being developed in Ottawa. I am informed that the fur producers believe such a federal research station is not required. So again I say, let us give more assistance to our dairy farmers, our hog farmers, our grain farmers and other agricultural producers. They are now receiving less government assistance and protection than farmers in almost any other developed nation.
That is not to say that the government has done nothing to help the farmers. More money than ever has been made available to provide farm loans and to assist credit sales
[Mr. Douglas (Assiniboia.l
of farm products. The Export Development Corporation was set up last session. Only about three months ago it was announced that our external food aid program was being increased $20 million, from $65 million to $85 million. Most of this aid consists of wheat and wheat flour. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) only a few days ago announced an increase of $1 million in the amount budgeted for feed grain freight assistance.
The government has appointed a minister to deal exclusively with the Wheat Board and the problems of the grain industry. Prairie farmers were pleased by the appointment of Saskatchewan's Otto Lang to that important position. I wish him well and assure him of my active support and assistance. He will have the constant and perhaps dubious benefit of my advice, solicited or otherwise, as he has already discovered.
I believe that one of the most significant things the government has done for the grain industry recently was the appointment of Mr. Charles Gibbings to fill a vacancy on the five-man Canadian Wheat Board. Ever since the Wheat Board was established by the Bennett government in the '30s, farmers and farm organizations have asked for farmer representation on the Wheat Board. Successive governments, including that headed by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), failed to comply with that request. Last July this government did appoint a farmer, so we at last have farmer representation on the Wheat Board-and not just any farmer; Mr. Gibbings was a practising grain farmer who was president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool for many years. He is probably one of the best known, most highly respected, and most [DOT]knowledgeable farmers in Canada, if not in the world. The government has not received as much credit for this very commendable appointment as I think it is entitled to, and I propose to try to rectify this omission at every opportunity.
Already I believe we can see positive results from this appointment. We have a new, unprecedented deferred delivery plan to take care of unequal delivery opportunities at the end of the crop year. We have an investigation within the Wheat Board of the whole operation of the quota system, which has had little revision since it was instituted 25 or 30 years ago. We are selling grain to new markets and reviving old ones. These are only a few of the results of this appointment. I take some credit for the initiation of some of these new policies.
November 3, 1969	COMMONS
Some hon. members opposite have accused the government of hampering the operations of the Wheat Board, of undermining it and trying to do away with it. This is absolutely not true. When the Standing Committee on Agriculture heard witnesses from the Wheat Board last spring one of the committee members asked if they would like any further assistance from the government. As I recall it, the reply was that they received the fullest co-operation and assistance from the government. May I remind hon. members that it was a Liberal government which two or three years ago introduced legislation establishing the Canadian Wheat Board on a permanent basis. Under previous governments it was set up on a renewable, five-year term, and every five years its enemies had an opportunity to press for its discontinuance. If any members of parliament are trying to undermine the Wheat Board, they are not in the Liberal ranks. I and the others on this side are 100 per cent behind the principle of the Canadian Wheat Board, Mr. Speaker.
I am the only western farmer on the Liberal side of this House of Commons with the exception of our Minister of Agriculture. Not only that, but I am the only farmer M.P. for any party from southern Saskatchewan. The hon. members for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh), Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Southam), Regina East (Mr. Burton), Regina Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) and Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) are urban men.

Consequently,
more and more people from all over southern Saskatchewan are coming to me with their problems. One of the problems which is affecting particularly Saskatchewan and Manitoba is the shortage of box cars and the inequitable distribution of the box cars that are available. I experience the effects of these conditions myself. Many farmers inside and outside of my constituency are complaining. The discriminatory treatment that some railway lines and some delivery points have been receiving is almost unbelievable.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why don't you do something about it?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am. As of October 24 some points had not received one box car since August 1. Many others had received one, two, three, four or five box cars. On favoured lines they have been getting plenty of cars, as many as 100, or more, at individual points.
DEBATES	445
The Address-Mr. A. B. Douglas
On October 22 I complained very loudly about these matters to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson). Within a week he had arranged for me to meet the top officials of the CNR and the CPR. We had an extremely frank exchange of opinions and ideas on October 29. I was able to present facts to bear out my contention that many farming communities are being very unfairly treated. An investigation into the general situation was promised. In particular, all concerned agreed that a concerted effort would be made to make space available for farmers to deliver the supplementary quotas on durum and barley which expire on November 28 next. Similar deadlines last year cut off delivery of supplementary quotas of durum and oats before all farmers had an opportunity to deliver; they were arbitrarily deprived of important income opportunities by the vagaries of box car distribution. Farmers thus treated were justifiably incensed, and I hope that such an outrage will not occur again this year.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Imagine what a labour union member or a bank shareholder would do if someone such as the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans), failed to deliver his pay cheque or dividend cheque. I am going to watch the box car supply and distribution situation closely for signs of the improvement which I hope will result from the meeting last week.
My friend and neighbour, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Southam), spoke in this debate last Wednesday. He had an advantage over me because he had just returned, armed with a great deal of material, from some sort of convention at Niagara Falls. His speech consisted largely of quotations from that material, although I do not believe that he made reference to the very interesting guaranteed income plan put forward by his leader but which was reportedly scuttled by a group of Tories led by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). By the way, the hon. member for Crowfoot must have exhausted himself in the scuttling operation because I noticed him in the house only briefly one day this session. Neither did the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain reveal his solution for the pressing problems of inflation to which I will refer in a few minutes if I have time.

You should be the minister of agriculture.
November 3, 1969

The Address-Mr. A. B. Douglas

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He did say something about the relative position of the United States in wheat exports compared with that of other countries, including Canada. He stated that in 1967-68 the U.S. increased its wheat exports while all other exporters lost ground, and total exports dropped by 12 per cent. This is true, and he probably knows why. The IGA expired on July 31, 1967, and the new IGA had not been ratified. So until it was ratified to become effective July 1, 1968, there was no floor price. The United States had no qualms about cutting prices, which was perfectly legal at that time. Canada, through our Wheat Board, tried to maintain prices to ensure that importers would ratify the agreement, because the agreement was probably more valuable and more important to Canada than to most other countries. I do not believe the hon. member protested this attitude at the time.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Your government sold us out at that time.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Perhaps Canada would have acted differently if present world wheat market conditions could have been foreseen. Up to that time it had been a sellers' market. In less than two years it has become a buyers' market and the hon. member's hindsight is marvellous to behold.
He should also have been using the latest figures available on page 5 of the August DBS publication, catalogue No. 22-005, which gives figures for 1968-69, the crop year just ended. Again, world wheat exports from the four major exporters listed dropped, this time by 18 per cent rather than the previous 12 per cent. The U.S. share dropped from 53.6 per cent in 1967-68 to 46.7 per cent. Canada's share went up from 24 per cent to 26.4 per cent. Why did he not give us the full picture?
He also berated the Minister of Agriculture for being realistic instead of blindly optimistic about grain markets in the next few years. I think it is far better to be a little pessimistic than to contribute to another cruel disillusionment such as has befallen grain farmers in the past two years. Farmers have so much built-in optimism that it does not require artificial stimulation. If they were not basically optimists they would all have quit the business years ago.
Recent statements by cabinet ministers, including the Minister of Agriculture and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, indicate that Soviet Russia intends very soon to enter negotiations regarding taking the balance of the 336-million bushel 1966 wheat

contract, and will also talk about further purchases. The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), who is still highly regarded in western Canada, recently made a trip to the Soviet Union. Perhaps he paid his own expenses, or perhaps the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) allocated to him part of the research funds which Parliament voted him. In any case, I am afraid it was not a very productive investment. It was pathetic, but not surprising, that the only announcement I heard him make on his return was a warmed-over version of what had been announced at the time of foreign secretary Gromyko's visit to Ottawa a few weeks ago and repeated several times since.
Further on the subject of wheat sales, the Wheat Board completed a very important wheat deal with Mainland China earlier this fall. Charles Gibbings was one of the three commissioners who spent some weeks in that country negotiating the sale. That sale was very encouraging to grain farmers who are now fairly confident that our exports this year will at least reach last year's level.
May I call it six o 'clock, Mr. Speaker.
