speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
before I interrupted myself at the dinner adjournment, among other things I had briefly reviewed some of the recent developments in wheat marketing, including the impending talks with Soviet Russia on the balance of the biggest wheat deal in history, a total sale of 336 million bushels negotiated by the Wheat Board under a Liberal government in 1966. The last item I mentioned was the large 82 million bushel, one-year agreement signed with Mainland China a few weeks ago.
In the statements on agricultural policy quoted by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain last Wednesday one can see the fine hand of that self-styled super-salesman, schoolteacher from Saskatchewan, Alvin Hamilton. He says he has the solution to our wheat surplus problem. If it is anything more than pure fantasy why does he not impart this precious knowledge to the Canadian
November 3, 1969

Wheat Board? He cannot hope to regain command of the Wheat Board for another three or four years at least. If he were really concerned about the welfare of grain farmers he would not conceal such valuable information and thereby allow the farmers to continue suffering from low quotas and low incomes. I submit he has no solution and that he is only trying to perpetuate a myth that he contrived to build up some years ago. The voters of Regina East called his bluff on June 25, 1968. It is rumoured that he made a trip to the Orient recently. If that is true his timing is not as good as it used to be. This time the big wheat sale had been announced some time before he got there. Or perhaps the difference is that he is no longer in a position to manipulate announcements until he can be on the spot.
We need some long-term planning for agriculture, Mr. Speaker. We need a national farm policy. Farmers hopefully await the final report of the Task Force on Agriculture which is expected before the end of 1969. In arriving at that final report members of the task force will have had the benefit of the discussions and conclusions at the history making agricultural congress held in Ottawa last March. A reliable blueprint for the future of agriculture is long overdue but I believe this new Trudeau government would have been open to criticism if a comprehensive farm policy had been announced without the benefit of this thorough study of farm problems. Also, the Canada Grains Council, which was established during the last session, has just started to function and should be able to contribute a valuable input to a national farm policy. So, Mr. Speaker, I look forward to the tabling of the task force report and to taking part in the development of agricultural policy and programs based on it.
Another report that we impatiently await is that on farm machinery costs. One of the recurring complaints at the meetings held by the Standing Committee on Agriculture in the prairies last spring was that of spiralling costs. In the many meetings I have attended since then, this remains one of the prime concerns. Our cash incomes are still comparatively high compared with 20 to 40 years ago, but our costs have risen astronomically. Farmers hope that the government's efforts to contain inflation, including the work of the Prices and Incomes Commission, will be effective in halting this unendurable cost-price squeeze which has bankrupted many already and which has brought most other grain farmers to the brink of insolvency.
The Address-Mr. Deakon
We fervently hope that the commission's attempts to obtain the necessary voluntary restraint from industry, unions and professional people are successful. The first apparent responses are not encouraging. The unions appear to be hostile to the idea of voluntary restraint. Industry is cool, with one of the pace-setters recently announcing steel price increases; and professional people, such as rural Saskatchewan teachers, are already campaigning for salary hikes in 1970.
The highly respected economist, John" Kenneth Galbraith, was reported to have said a couple of weeks ago that he could see no alternative than for the governments of Canada and the United States to impose strict price and wage controls on at least the major North American industries and trade unions. If the alternative to such control is mounting inflation followed by a terrific depression, which I am afraid is the most likely prospect, I am all in favour of such controls, and the sooner the better. I believe that most people on the prairies feel the same way.
In my opinion the Speech from the Throne was a very fine document. It is encouraging to know that the government is concerned about the strengthening of the United Nations, which I believe should be one of the top priorities. I eagerly look forward to the progressive legislation planned, including items to lower the voting age, to revise the Canada Grain Act, to increase grain sales, to reform taxes, to control and preserve our water resources, to reform criminal law, to protect consumers, to provide more low income housing and to improve labour-management relations.
Last but not least, I see much evidence in the Speech from the Throne and in actions and words of our Prime Minister and various other Ministers, that the government is genuinely concerned about the serious problems of Canadian farmers and is doing something about them. Mr. Speaker, I shall support the motion.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, on rising to take part in this debate may I first concur with other hon. members of the House in congratulating the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau). Before proceeding with my comments on the Speech from the Throne may I bring to the attention of hon. members the fact that the federal riding of
November 3, 1969

The Address-Mr. Deakon High Park which I have the honour to represent is, through redistribution, composed of parts of the old ridings of York Humber, York South, York West and High Park. It is a most diversified riding economically and contains residents of a mosaic of ethnic origins.
May I take this opportunity to congratulate my predecessor, Mr. A. J. P. Cameron, for conscientious and unselfish dedication to this institution during his many years of service here and wish him well in his future endeavours. May I also express my deep regret and condolences to the family of the former member for York West, Hon. Robert Winters, on his sudden passing. His great contributions to Canada's economy and our democratic institutions shall long be remembered. He was indeed a great Canadian.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take the short time available to me to briefly enunciate a few of my opinions on the Speech from the Throne. It was regrettable that the Speech from the Throne did not contain a greater priority in respect of urban affairs. Today, when more than 80 per cent of our nation's population resides in large cities such as Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver, Winnipeg, Halifax and others, from whence the majority of our problems arise necessitating legislation in transport, health, manpower, welfare, housing, consumer affairs, criminal law and communications, to name but a few, it would appear that our government does not consider this to be a major priority.
I know that the majority of those who do not agree with my statement will fall back on the excuse that this is not within the jurisdiction of the federal government and is a provincial and municipal matter. This is partially correct; but I submit it takes in all levels of government, as can be illustrated by some opinions advanced by a group of builders with whom I had the privilege to discuss the question of housing. They classified their difficulties in the following manner. First, municipal governments are maintaining outdated, archaic and restrictive building codes and demanding outdated building methods and materials. They hedge on re-zoning in areas where housing would be possible. In some cases builders are held up for more than three years by local councils. The builders' overheads, taxes and interest on the land are all added to the cost of the lot for which the home buyer eventually pays. I am advised that land costs now account for approximately one-third of the total cost of a home.
IMr. Deakon.]
Second, provincial governments have not made land available to the builders. As an example in Ontario one can cite the Thistle-town and Malvern land projects. Third, I submit that the federal government has been causing trouble for our builders in that it has make their work uncertain and difficult by an uncertain and fluctuating mortgage loan policy, to the point where builders cannot plan ahead. A builder is required to hire a large staff just in case more units can be permitted to be constructed and this increases his overhead and the ultimate cost 'of a home. Costs are also added since he can only construct one, two or three buildings at a time instead of introducing a whole assembly program which could bring about a large saving by the elimination of waste material and labour.
This is one example of overlapping jurisdiction and, therefore, of the constitutional argument. But the average man on the street has not one gram of knowledge about constitutional ramifications. All he knows is that he needs shelter at an economical cost; he needs food, clothing and medical attention for himself and his family. So let us take the bull by the horns, provide leadership, co-ordinate the efforts of all levels of government and endeavour to resolve some of these problems confronting the urban dweller. If we do not do this and we do not have jurisdiction, let us not abdicate our responsibilities in this regard Let us allow the provinces to do the job and distribute our finances to them on a per capita basis. The cities and urban centres are the pulse and heartbeat of our nation. I am therefore in agreement with the hon. member for York West (Mr. Givens) and would respectfully recommend that the government set up a standing committee of this House to deal with urban affairs.
Another issue on which I hold strong views is that of the sovereignty of our northern waters. This question has within the past few months come to the fore with the voyage of the Manhattan through the northwest passage; yet our government does not consider that these recent developments constitute a threat to Canada's sovereignty over her Arctic waters. This is indeed an optimistic point of view since one need only refer to the United States state department which has openly stated that the United States regards Lancaster Sound, Prince of Wales Strait, McClure Strait and other channels which comprise the northwest passage to be international waterways.
November 3, 1SG9
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if we do not take a strong stand now and snap out of our lethargy, we may lose by default. We must immediately take steps to assert our sovereignty by increasing our patrols by ship and aircraft over the Arctic waters. We must set up regulations with reasonable requirements as to the use of proper equipment and safe navigational practices for ships travelling the northwest passage. We must also set down stringent conditions in order to control pollution.
I had the privilege, with other colleagues of this House, of visiting the northern Arctic. We had the opportunity of going to the spot where apparently one of the large barges had been sunk. The barge contained high test airplane fuel which had apparently leaked out and evaporated, but it still contained approximately 110,000 gallons of diesel fuel. I do not know all the details of the operation, but apparently the barge had been moved and sunk at a depth of approximately 200 fathoms. I submit that because the barge is made of metal it will in a very short time corrode in the salt water. Eventually the pressure of the water will cause the barge to burst and a lot of diesel fuel will seep out and pollute large areas of the Canadian Arctic.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I am pleased to know the Prime Minister has indicated that the government will be taking some steps in this direction but I respectfully submit this is not sufficient for the following reasons. First, circumstances at present favour a stronger stand since it has been proven that even ships as massive as the Manhattan cannot penetrate the northwest passage without the assistance of powerful icebreakers and expert help. Canada has both expert help and the icebreakers to do the job. Second, by such methods as those I have recommended, Russia has acquired control over its northern sea route. Third, Mr. Speaker, we need not be too concerned if we carry out the previous suggestions as to asserting our control, and should we be challenged about our claim the subject matter would be adjudicated by the International Court of Justice of the United Nations. Three of the nations represented on the court are Japan, Britain and the Philippines, all of which are island nations and have a vital interest in maintaining control over the sea channels between their islands. I believe, therefore, that we can count on them for a sympathetic hearing. I therefore support the other hon. members of this House, Mr. Speaker, who are
The Address-Mr. Deakon in favour of the Government of Canada formally declaring the Arctic channels to be Canadian territorial waters.
Although the National Advisory Council on Fitness and Amateur Sport has made a number of studies regarding amateur sport in Canada, there is still a great deal more which can be done, especially on the general subject of minor hockey, its mushrooming pee-wee tournaments, its contribution to the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association and its numerous financial problems. At present, if it were not for the large number of volunteers who unselfishly give of their time we would not have the calibre of athletes we have today. If we are to remain in international competition and are concerned about the frustrations of today's youth, we must immediately take steps to promote, encourage and financially assist these sports. I commend the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) for his part in the establishment of the cross-Canada sports demonstration project. This is a step in the right direction, but there is a great deal more that can be done.
I have listened to numerous speeches in this House by hon. members opposite, implying that they are the only ones concerned about old age pensioners and others on fixed incomes. Let me just reiterate that we on this side of the House also have a genuine concern for the old, needy and less fortunate, and I trust that the government will be taking steps to rectify these inequalities. There are numerous other matters which require urgent legislation. Notably among them are bankruptcy regulations and a revision of our immigration laws. I intend to speak on these subjects at a later date.
Taking the cue from other members and thinking it might be advisable to involve the general public in our legislation, I distributed a questionnaire to my constituents, the results of which have been tabulated. I think they might be of interest to hon. members present. I would like to have these questions and answers placed on the record. They are as follows: Should Canada recognize Red China? Yes, 60.3 per cent; no, 29.9 per cent; no opinion, 9.8 per cent. Is Canada taking sufficient steps to protect its sovereignty in the north? Yes, 13.9 per cent; no, 70.9 per cent; no opinion, 15.2 per cent. Would you agree to wage and price controls? Yes, 70 per cent; no, 24.3 per cent; no opinion, 5.7 per cent. Should a guaranteed income become the basis of a revised welfare program? Yes, 41.7 per cent; no, 48 per cent; no opinion, 10.3 per cent. Should family allowances be paid to only

November 3, 1969

The Address-Mr. Valade those below a specified income level? Yes, 69.4 per cent; no, 25.7 per cent; no opinion, 4.9 per cent. Should cigarette smoking be banned? Yes, 59.3 per cent; no, 28.9 per cent; no opinion, 11.8 per cent. Should the sale and use of marijuana be controlled on a similar basis to alcohol? Yes, 62.5 per cent; no, 27.6 per cent; no opinion, 9.9 per cent. Should old age pensions be geared to the cost of living index? Yes, 96 per cent; no, 2.2 per cent; no opinion, 1.8 per cent. Should a more uniform sentencing system be instituted? Yes, 83.8 per cent; no, 11.2 per cent; no opinion, 5.8 per cent. Should our tax reform program include a capital gains tax? Yes, 59.7 per cent; no, 29.8 per cent, no opinion, 10.5 per cent.
Legislation must be passed to control inflation even if it maintains wages at their present level? Yes, 74.8 per cent; no, 16.9 per cent; no opinion, 8.3 per cent. More effective and stringent bankruptcy laws should be passed immediately? Yes, 82.7 per cent; no,, 3.5 per cent; no opinion, 13.8 per cent. Criminal records should be expunged after five years? Yes, 49.8 per cent; no, 36.9 per cent; no opinion, 13.3 per cent. The bail system should be placed on a more equitable basis? Yes, 77.3 per cent; no, 9.2 per cent; no opinion, 13.5 per cent.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, this is a most significant survey because a very large number of the questionnaires were returned. In many instances the people who returned them wrote three or four pages of comment on other subjects. This clearly demonstrates that the public are interested in our institutions.
In conclusion may I say in all sincerity that notwithstanding these aforementioned criticisms, the government should be commended for proposing the reduction of the voting age to 18, setting up programs to reduce regional disparities, proposing tax reform and improving and preserving our water resources, to name but a few. I trust that with the co-operation of our amicable opposition the coming session will be a productive one.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to custom, I should like to join with the hon. members who have already contributed to the debate to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, and this, for several reasons: first, because with rather clever dialectics they managed to gloss over the disappointment felt by the Canadian

people following that Speech from the Throne, since it provided them with very little relief.
Also, I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member who had the floor before me for the inquiries he carried out to prove that he had heard many complaints against the present government in his constituency. In fact, his findings show that the government has failed in the Speech from the Throne to consider the urgent problems of the day.
Despite the 71 legislative proposals, the speech offers very few concrete measures to solve the kind of problems which the hon. member has just mentioned.
I went through the list of the 71 bills submitted by this government in its Speech from the Throne which I would define as follows: an exercise in academic rhetoric more remarkable by the number than by the quality of its proposals.
Needless to say that I examined the contents and the scope of these 71 bills. I find, as every hon. member must have, that 38 are designed to amend existing legislation and that 22 only are new proposals, few of which are really important.
Such is, Mr. Speaker, the performance of a government which promised not only to create a just society, but also to examine concretely the problems Canadians are facing. And yet in its second year in office an opportunity was afforded to it to settle Canada's urgent problems through legislation.
However, as we have found out, there is no indication of any measure to control and promote the development of family housing.
No measure is introduced to restrict and restrain inflation.
The interest rate is left unregulated. People are wondering if they are to continue paying interests at the rate of 9, 10, 11 and 12 percent and if the government will let this plague worsen, since it neutralizes all the home building industry in Canada.
Furthermore, the cost of living is still increasing. In this connection, someone was telling me that during a recent trip to Edmonton he had paid 79 cents for a piece of steak that costs $1.69 on the Montreal market.
Those are only a few examples of what people are really interested in.
In the proposed bills, there is no provision for air and water pollution control. Nothing indicates either that the government intends to legislate on drug control

I am referring to
November 3, 1969

psychedelic drugs, marijuana and other related drugs-the use of which is really dangerous for our youth.
Moreover, no reference is made to the possibility of improving the postal service in spite of the rates increases implemented last year. Nothing new is proposed in the constitutional field, in spite of growing tensions in federal-provincial relations. We are not given to understand that attempts will be made to settle problems which require an urgent solution because they threaten the structure of our country at this time.
The throne speech makes no mention of measures to eradicate the plague of unemployment that particularly affects Quebec and the Maritimes. The minister himself said recently that there was an 8 per cent unemployment rate in Quebec and I was most surprised to hear the seconder of the Address in reply say very sincerely and perhaps naively, as the tyro making one of his first speeches in the House, that the unemployment rate in his riding was 14 per cent.
If that is the situation, I think government members should recognize the importance of those matters and ask the government to act immediately instead of eternally delaying the necessary legislation.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, we would also have liked to reconsider welfare pensions and others. We all know-and I think that the hon. members opposite also know it-that it is impossible today for our older citizens, those who have reached a venerable age and who live on welfare allowances, to live decently due to all kinds of increases. That is why, like most Canadians, I am so deeply disappointed by the Speech from the Throne which does not let us foresee any improvement in the lot and condition of the aged.
Nor is there, Mr. Speaker, anything to indicate that the angry outbursts of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) against the C.B.C. will have any effect if there is no follow-up to his public criticism. The Prime Minister blurted out those words during an enthusiastic and congenial meeting of Liberals, and we may well wonder whether he did mean them, whether he was merely carried away or again whether he was threatening in some way certain persons in the C.B.C. who had offended him or who had refused to give him their support in the last election.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
It remains that if the government has no intention to pass legislation in order to
The Address

Mr. Valade change certain elements of the internal structure and certain operating methods of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, we can only wonder whether it intends to take direct action as it did in laying off employees earning an average salary instead of going after the management of this state-owned company.
We must deal with issues of great current interest, such as the present economic situation in Canada and the measures the government intends to take in order to restore order, respect for the law and security in Canada.
I have greatly appreciated the contribution made by hon. members in particular the seriousness and the interest which they often displayed in their remarks on Canadian problems. Even if the government members obviously do it to protect the government, I think that on the whole hon. members discharged their responsibilities in a competent and honest manner.
In my opinion, the most important problem in Canada is surely that of the economy. Every day, we hear about the plague of regional disparity and of the dangers ensuing from it.
Regional disparities make it possible for people in one province to have more than a sufficient income allowing them to live in comfort and prosperity while in other areas some citizens live in the most abject poverty.
I was wondering what were the reasons for those regional disparities. Of course, we must rely on the initiative of the government which has promised a great number of measures in that field but has yet to do something about it.
We were recently given a small pamphlet featuring a mid-year review and the 1969 outlook for private and public investments in Canada. It contains statistics on investments and capital expenditures for the second term of the current fiscal year. Referring to the figures appearing on page 6 of the pamphlet, I shall draw a parallel with the investments and capital expenditures of recent years. For instance, the Atlantic provinces show an increase of 11 per cent in capital expenditures over 1968. In the other provinces, increases over 1968 were as follows: Quebec, 5 per cent; Ontario, 16 per cent; Prairies, 6 per cent and British Columbia, 12 per cent.
There are clearly disparities in the capital expenditures and investments of lower levels of government. What particularly struck me is that in this economic report, for statistical purposes, Canada is divided into five regions,

November 3, 1969
The Address-Mr. Valade i.e. the Atlantic region, Quebec, Ontario, the Prairies and British Columbia.
I wish to recall a statement made by the premier of one of the provinces during a constitutional conference. In order to solve the problem of regional disparities, I wonder whether the Standing Committee on the Constitution might not look fully into the advantages of dividing Canada into five regions, each of which would correspond to economic realities, so as to minimize political differences that quite often stem from economic causes.
I know of course that some people have been opposed to this idea for very good reasons, whether of a local or regional nature. If we, the representatives of the people who are here to deal with the problems, do not eliminate the root causes of conflict or of regional disparities, if we are afraid, if we shrink from the imperative necessity of dealing, in a drastic way perhaps, with such problems, we should not be surprised to see our country disintegrate and thousands of Canadians suffer from the inaction of the government and from the inefficiency of the laws, because the mechanism that is proposed to solve the problems is not what it could be if we reviewed provincial boundaries, to make of the provinces economic entities which could, of course, at the same time, correspond to political realities.
Having said this, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to a remark made in this house during the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
Someone has referred to the role that a member should play. Very often, hon. members say in the newspapers, on television or directly to their constituents: I am just a member, I cannot do anything. In the house, at least, it may seem that I have no influence, but I do express the views of my constituents at the party caucus.
I think that the time has come, more than ever, for hon. members to stop pretending, in conferences or meetings with their electors, that they act within the caucus. We all know that a lot of work is accomplished in the caucus. All of us also know that each individual member has his heart set on representing his riding within his party. However, I think that when a member is elected it is to express here in this house the needs, the opinions and the hopes of those who elected him. I wish to see some day the disappearance of such an easy excuse which several members may use at times.

Hon. members have received a mandate. They cannot discharge that mandate if they only make themselves heard within the caucus. They ought to do it in the house. That excuse which we use too often may perhaps be traced back to the famous standing order 75C which restricts the length of the debates in the house, therefore preventing too often a member from participating in the debates and making known the opinions, the hopes and the problems of the people in his riding.
We are living now in Canada, and especially in the province of Quebec, unprecedentedly grave hours. We have come to the point where we often wonder-and the public also-what on earth we are doing and what is the point of having governments. A majority of the Canadian people are urging government members, parliament members, public servants at every level of government to open 'their eyes to the deplorable condition now prevailing and to take the necessary steps and legislation to prevent the country from collapsing into unrest and anarchy.
It is high time for the men in public life to make up their minds and to take action thus ensuring the respect of law and order in Canada and guaranteeing the future safety of every Canadian citizen in every province of Canada, from Halifax to Vancouver.
* (8:50 p.m.)
Never, Mr. Speaker, has our society been threatened more than it is today. Its social structure is threatened, as is the family as a unit.
The disturbances which of late have become more frequent in my province worry even the most optimistic.
When union leaders and teachers extol the overthrow by force of the powers that be to children of 9, 10, 11 or 12 years of age, and undermine family authority through revolutionary indoctrination, when the call to violence becomes the modus vivendi of the student body, the authorities and the governments have not only the right but the imperious duty to intervene.
Even if such things happen more often in Quebec, it does not mean that this situation is confined to that province.
One needs not be a pessimist to notice the progressive and steady disintegration of the Canadian society, but rather a realist and a clearsighted person.
Every Canadian citizen is partly responsible for building a better society as well as for the present disorder.
November 3, 1969

Rulers should be able to face up to ringleaders, professional agitators, and anarchists, too often imported in Canada because of permissive legislation.
If every Canadian citizen must contribute to restore order, justice and the respect for the law, it is also the imperious duty of governments to intervene. The example, as the saying goes, must come from high up. Nothing is more true and more realistic at the present time.
It is not enough for the Prime Minister to fly into a violent temper over the national TV network, before his supporters. This can only be harmful, and likely to lessen the respect that everyone must have for the high office he holds.
Mr. Speaker, to close one's eyes and to pretend that things will settle with time is to sit on an erupting volcano.
For too long the Prime Minister of Canada has ignored or made light of the many warnings that were given to him, both in this house and outside. When tolerance, Mr. Speaker, turns to flabbiness, when liberalism becomes licence and political dogma obliterates authority, sweeping reforms are needed to prevent a disaster.
The federal and provincial governments must enforce strict laws to ensure the security of citizens and some respect for their individual and collective rights.
In Canada, the word "democracy" has been used so widely that its limitations have been forgotten.
The government must ensure through adequate and efficient pieces of legislation that the Department of Manpower and Immigration will not open its doors wide to professional revolutionaries. It must ensure that our Criminal Code imposes the capital punishment to those who will advocate through violence the upsetting of democratic law and order. The seditious act should be more clearly defined in the Criminal Code.
Mr. Speaker, if we are not completely blind or criminally slothful and if authorities do not react, we are surely heading for what I would call the "Canadian dilemma".
If we do not take strong and immediate action, if our society does not wake up, we will be faced with the following alternatives: McCarthyism or communism; dictatorship or anarchy; censorship or licentiousness; economic control or recession with its disastrous consequences.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps those who will say that I am a pessimist or something of the 21362-30
The Address-Mr. Valade kind have too soon forgotten the Sir George Williams University affair, the riots which occurred at the time of the Montreal police strike and the events now taking place in the province of Quebec.
I certainly wish, Mr. Speaker, that my predictions are exaggerated and unrealistic. Only time will tell. It is up to us to act so that those predictions do not become an irreversible political reality.
To fill in the cracks which are beginning to show in the structure of our society, politicians must have a sense of responsibility.
The agitators of whom I spoke earlier take advantage of the constitutional problems and the political clashes between Quebec and Ottawa. The Prime Minister of Canada must stop providing the agitators with weapons through his irresponsible statements.
Is it necessary, and I ask the question seriously, for the Prime Minister of Canada to stand as the uncompromising opponent of Quebec in order to maintain his popularity?
By its negative aggressiveness, its unconsidered responses towards Quebec and its government, by the refusal of the Prime Minister to hold a dialogue on matters deemed essential by Quebec, the federal government emphasizes the Quebecers' distrust of Ottawa and French-Canadian members sitting here. In addition, it provides with arguments those who only try to justify their anarchy.
The purely political matters are not the only devices to which agitators will resort in Canada.
The head of a family who is unable to provide for the essential needs of his children is an easy prey for those people.
Quebec is restless? Yes, it is true!
Economically speaking, Quebec faces great difficulties at the present time. Unemployment has reached dangerous levels.
Recently, His Eminence Cardinal Leger, on a visit to Canada, reminded us of this selfevident truth that the distance separating the rich from the poor is still growing.
In Montreal, Canada's metropolis, there are cases of dire poverty, cases of extreme hardship, which we in public life who are responsible for the government of the country have no right to ignore or to tolerate in a self-styled just society.
This distance, Mr. Speaker, it is the duty of all of us and of the government to reduce it. Half-measures are no longer acceptable.
454	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Valade
Let us postpone the adoption of less important legislation such as the omnibus bill and others of the same type. Let us settle the urgent problems: housing, the cost of living, employment; social measures allowing people on relief to live decently.
I heard the hon. member who spoke before me say that he too was concerned with the problems of older people and that he supported the government in that respect.
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. members on the government side realized in what exceedingly difficult situation live older people with no other income than their meager old-age pension, they would quickly understand that those people who are still able to do countless things for their follow-citizens, cannot live, cannot eat three meals a day with the meager allowances we grant them at present under our social legislation.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Let us not delude ourselves, Mr. Speaker, and tell these people that the government cannot increase these allowances because it would run into more debts, that it cannot afford it and that we are living in a period of austerity.
Mr. Speaker, should I be asked to choose between an increase of $200 million a year for welfare and old age pensions or the C.B.C.,
I would sacrifice the $200 million for the C.B.C. and earmark that amount for the old people of our country who are only waiting for assistance and perhaps a little gratefulness from their government representatives.
Mr. Speaker, let us give our young people positive options for the future. Let us see to it that they escape narcotics and psychedelic drugs and their after effects.
Recently, I was reading an article in La Presse-and I think all the newspapers have published this news item, relating to a very sad case that has to do with the daughter of a famous American comedian, and I mention him by name, since it is a well-known fact, I mean Mr. Art Linkletter who devoted all his life to the young people and made a most interesting career out of it. In this article from La Presse, Mr. Linkletter said:
My daughter did not commit suicide. It is the makers and peddlers of LSD who murdered her. She was not herself.
I suggest this is an indictment for murder, on the part of a father who lost one of his beloved daughters.
Should such a calamity befall one of us, we would unhesitatingly request the government

DEBATES	November 3, 1969
to take immediate drastic action to exercise control over these narcotics which are leading our youth to their destruction.
I am confident that if we provide young people with the necessary leadership, bring them up with sound principles and a healthy outlook, show them that their parliamentary representatives have their interests at heart, they will resist contamination by the bane of narcotics.
Mr. Speaker, I feel sure that if we prepare young people for the future not through anarchy and chaos but with due respect for law and order, then in spite of the present unpleasant situation, there will be a better future for Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first like to congratulate my colleague the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) who moved the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, and my colleague the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) who in seconding the Address did great service to his constituency by drawing attention to the size of the blueberries grown there. I am sure all lovers of blueberry pie will appreciate his remarks. May I also congratulate those hon. members who were recently appointed to the cabinet or to the position of parliamentary secretary. The choice of individuals to fill these positions was in my opinion most appropriate. I know they will distinguish themselves in the fulfilment of their duties.
Despite the remarks of certain members of the opposition to the effect that the Speech from the Throne was filled with pious platitudes liberally interlaced with empty promises, I, together with many people in my constituency, find the Speech from the Throne to be a document which has encouraged the people of Canada to look forward to a constructive session of Parliament. Today I should like to speak to one specific item. I refer to the proposal to lower the voting age to 18. This proposed move on the part of the government involves many
November 3, 1963

implications. It is a recognition of youth and the part youth has played and is playing in the Canada of today, and will play in the Canada of tomorrow. Youth has an interest in government. This was evident in the last election when youth joined the ranks of all political parties throughout Canada. This aspect of the campaign was especially evident in my riding. In my opinion it was one of the highlights of the campaign on all sides, indeed, it added a new dimension and injected new life and enthusiasm.
The youth of today are vitally interested in the affairs of the nation. They express themselves in many ways, some of which are not constructive. Everyone, including youth, has the right to protest, but with that protest there must be responsibility. A democratic society is not based upon force and the destruction of property, looting and causing bodily harm to others. By lowering the voting age the government is bringing youth into the mainstream of decision-making. Although at times they may feel their part and the influence of their individual ballot is small, nevertheless they will be aware they no longer are on the sidelines but are taking a part in their country's affairs. It will not be long before they become aware it is the cumulative effort of many people casting their ballots for a cause that creates action and has its effect on society.
A corollary to the lowering of the voting age is the present attitude of people and government toward youth and the effect that some of their actions have upon* youth. One of these is the reduction in the size of our reserve forces. Most members of this House will heartily endorse the action of the government in its effort to fight inflation by cutting back expenditures. I believe, however, that the reserve force is one area in which serious consideration should be given to a no-cut policy. Through the militia, as it was formerly called, thousands of young Canadians have over the years received important, useful training which has made them better citizens. The reserve forces have provided physical and mental stimulation as well as moral development. It has been brought to my attention that the dollar investment in the reserve forces yields one of the greatest returns for the money spent. I subscribe to this opinion because a large percentage of the members of the reserve forces are in the high school and university age group. The pay received has assisted students to continue their education and has provided summer employment 21362-30$
The Address-Mr. Whiting through participation in summer courses of up to eight weeks' duration.
When speaking of the reserve forces I must point out that the militia has been the vital fibre from which our armed forces have stemmed in every national emergency. This was true at the beginning of World War I, the Second World War and the Korean war in 1950. It was from the militia that our forces drew their original strength. The militia formed the nucleus of our fighting power at that time. Although we hope and pray that this need may never recur, the reserves have always performed a patriotic duty in the preservation of Canada as a nation. So Canadians owe more than a debt of gratitude to the reserve forces. If anything were done to diminish their effectiveness or curtail their activities a Canadian image which has been created through patriotism, hard work and dedication, it would be deplored in the hearts of many loyal Canadians.
Although we must be guided by a principle which ensures fairness and equality in reducing national expenditures, nevertheless there are extenuating circumstances which must guide the consideration accorded certain plans. This has already been done in the case of regional development. In my opinion the reserve force is another example which should be accorded special consideration. I have referred to its importance in relation to youth, I have talked about the part the reserve has played in national emergencies and I have mentioned the opportunity for patriotic expression associated with this organization which has been built through dedication to our country over its years of existence.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I have not talked about the contribution the reserve army makes and can make to our over-all defence when our regular forces are reduced. Our reserve forces are a source of trained men ready for action; they are ready should there be need to defend our borders, or to handle local disorders should they arise. The reserves are also a source of personnel for the regular forces. The cost of training and the time required for training a man who has had the benefit of reserve instruction is much less than that required for the training of a raw recruit. But how much money are we talking about in the cost of operating the reserve force? It is less than 2 per cent of the defence budget. We must weigh this cost against the achievements of the reserve force, its potential and its function, and once again I would like to place special emphasis on the
456	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. MacGuigan part it plays and the interest it has for the youth of our country.
Some time ago an airline company came up with the slogan "Fly now, pay later". I think the endeavours of governments, led by the federal government, to reduce expenditures is commendable but there are areas wherein a variation of that slogan might apply. I suggest "Cut now, pay later". I also suggest that this is more a truism than a slogan when considered in connection with many of the programs concerning youth.
One of my reasons for focussing attention on youth was prompted by an event which took place in my home town of Oakville last week. It was Police Appreciation Week. The week was planned to give the public an opportunity to better understand the workings of the police department and, as might be expected, much attention was focussed on their work with youth. Police Chief Fred Oliver said in an interview that dealing with youth is not a cost but an investment. It is not true that teenagers are not good; the majority of teenagers are good. His opinion applied to more than 95 per cent of our youth.
At the same time Inspector Fern Alexander, one of Canada's few women police inspectors and head of the metro Toronto youth bureau, said that by the end of this year in metro Toronto 30,000 young people will have been in trouble with the law and 20 per cent of those will be around to haunt us for a long time. There will never be enough money to provide phsychiatrists, psychologists and other properly trained people to handle the situation. It is through participation that we can develop the full potential of our youth. Lowering the voting age to 18 gives them the opportunity to participate in government. Maintaining a vital reserve force gives the government an opportunity to participate in the building of character and the development of youth.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to join those of my colleagues who have already expressed their congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address in Keply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau). These hon. members have set a fine example to those of us who were elected in 1968 and have provided us with a fine example in trying to equal their efforts.
I would also like to extend my congratulations to hon. members of the House who
fMr. Whiting.]
DEBATES	November 3, 1969
recently had new duties bestowed upon them, the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) and the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), for their elevation to governmental rank, and the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) and the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) for their well merited promotion to the rank of parliamentary secretary. I would like in particular to extend my congratulations to my close neighbour, the hon. member for Windsor West who, as a result of seven years' assiduous service in this house marked by careful attention to detail in all the activities of government, has now succeeded in establishing himself as one of that select group of people who present policy to this house. The city of Windsor is fortunate in having two such able cabinet representatives as the hon. member for Windsor West and the hon. Senator for Windsor-Walkerville.
One theme of the Throne Speech, and the principal theme in subsequent discussion, has been the necessity of controlling inflation. The rate of inflation in this country has been running at about 5 per cent this year and about 4 per cent in the years immediately preceding. We are far from the worst off country in the world, of course. In Chile the rate of inflation is about 35 per cent and in Brazil it is over 20 per cent. The United States and most other industrialized countries of the world, except Germany, have a rate of inflation which is higher than that of Canada. But we cannot for this reason comfortably conclude that our inflation arises solely from external causes, that is, from world causes over which we may have very little control.
The very fact of the differing rates in the various countries of the world from a high of 35 per cent to a low of 2 or 3 per cent shows that native conditions and national governmental policies have a good deal to do with the rate of inflation. We therefore have the duty to examine our own government, our own society and our own economic structure to see if there are ways in which we in Canada can combat this very serious problem independently of the efforts which are also being made by countries such as the United States to deal with it. This is just what our government has been doing. Our attempts to control inflation have been based on fiscal and monetary policies, on the beginning of the operation of the Prices and Incomes Commission and on an attempt to combat the inflation psychology which some economists and many psychologists tell us in one of the
November 3, 1969
most important aspects of the problem of inflation.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The government's austerity program is a very important part of the whole program of confining inflation to reasonable limits. What else can we do that we have not been doing up to this point? In my opinion the Prices and Incomes Commission should not be a mere fact finding body but should rather be a judgmental body. It should not be one which merely informs the people of what has been happening, but one which passes judgment on those events that have been happening. Of course, we have been distressed in the last few weeks by the large increase in the price of steel following upon, although not necessarily caused by, the wage settlement which was obtained by the United Steelworkers in the negotiations at Hamilton.
Dr. Kenneth Galbraith, our famous Canadian expatriot, last week, expressed the view in this city that one of the serious causes of inflation was the confrontation between the strong corporation and the strong union. Union demands are met by the corporation and then prices are raised to pass the increase in wages along to the consumer. The danger, as Galbraith and many other economists have pointed out, is that the corporation will use wage increases as an excuse for price increases which perhaps it had planned anyway, in order to raise once again the return on the corporation's investment.
I do not agree with one hon. member opposite who was speaking last week of corporate profits and said that because we have a continuing high rate of return on corporate investment this necessarily shows that something is wrong. After all, interest rates have been increasing in our economy generally and it is no surprise in such circumstances that corporate returns on capital have not been dropping and in some cases have been increasing. But at the same time we need to scrutinize very carefully price increases which are made by corporations, especially in industries where there is very little real competition between corporate giants, and again especially in industries which are very basic, bellwether industries if you like for our economy. In such industries we ought to have very careful examination, by a body such as the Prices and Incomes Commission, of any price increases which have occurred and, if necessary, of any wage settlements which have been made.
The Address-Mr. MacGuigan
The Prices and Incomes Commission should feel free to look at all the economic events that are happening in our society which relate to prices and incomes, to inform us about them and to make judgments upon them, not as a substitute for members of this House but as an aid to the judgment of the-members here. It seems to me that while this; in itself might not prove sufficient to control completely the problem of inflation, it would be going considerably beyond where we are now and would be a step considerably short of that of complete wage and price control.
The second alternative that we have is the alternative of wage and price control. Hon. members know, Mr. Speaker, that in the Board of Commerce Act case decided almost 50 years ago by the Privy Council, that august but often mistaken judicial body decided that it was not within the power of the federal government of this country to have a prices and wages policy which would impose prices and wages on industry.
It may be that this was a wrong decision. Many legal authorities believe that it was. It may also be that the Supreme Court of Canada, now our highest judicial body, would be prepared at this point in our history to overrule that earlier decision because most of the law of that period, most of the dicta of the cases which limited the trade and commerce power and the peace, order and good government power in our constitution, has since been disowned either by later Privy Council decisions or by the Supreme Court of Canada itself since it became the final court of appeal in 1949. It may be that this earlier decision could be successfully challenged and that, strictly on legal grounds, we could begin now to have wage and price controls, but I would suggest this would probably not be the most fruitful way to proceed. This is a case which has stood for some 45 to 50 years. It. has been relied upon by people in this country since that time. It would probably be much better if we were to attempt, as I believe government spokesmen have suggested, to bring about a political solution through a conference, seeking provincial agreement either to having the constitution of this country changed permanently to allow the federal government to set up real prices and wages control, or to work out some co-operative mechanism which would enable the two levels of government to work together to solve the problem.
From the comments of provincial governments and provincial ministers of finance it seems that the provincial governments are

November 3, 1969

The Address-Mr. MacGuigan just as seriously concerned about this problem as is our own government, and I think we could anticipate that if we were to use political means we might work out a solution. But, Mr. Speaker, the fact that we could work out such a solution does not mean we should leap to this step. It is a very extreme step in a democratic society. It is one which is very hard to make work, and is especially hard to make work in the light of the frame of mind in our society which itself causes inflation.
We have inflation in part because people do not believe it is a time in which they are called upon to make any particular sacrifices for the government of our country. They see no reason why they should not demand higher wages, why prices should not rise when they are not being affected, and in their personal decisions it would seem they do not have uppermost the demands of the common good. With such a popular state of mind it would be extremely difficult to get the support that would be necessary to make a prices and wages board which would impose compulsory restraints on our society work very well. ' Whichever of these methods we choose-and my own feeling is that we will have to find other methods than the ones we are now using before this problem is fully controlled-I am confident we will succeed in controlling inflation, if only because we cannot afford to fail.
Now I am going to say a few words about the economic situation from a different point of view, from the point of view of what I would consider to be justified exceptions to the government's austerity program. The Speech from the Throne recognizes several of these. One is that programs to reduce regional disparities in employment opportunities and incomes will not be subject to the general austerity program. Indeed, the Speech says that governmental expenditure in this area will be increased because of the priority which the government rightly assigns to this very serious problem.
The Speech from the Throne also points out that the housing program to construct one million units over the next five years, combined with a recognition of the paramount importance of low income housing, will also be exempted from the general austerity program. I would like to suggest two further exceptions which I believe ought to be made to the general program of austerity. The first of these is with respect to superannuated civil servants. From time to time it has been said that these retired employees are in no worse position than retired employees under plans

of private industry where those plans have been outdistanced by inflation. I think this is true, but I also think that the government has a particular responsibility with respect to those citizens who have been its employees. It cannot very well insist that employees of corporations have the right to receive from those corporations additional remuneration over and above that which is provided by contract under the original agreement with their employer. But it can, as an act of gratuity in the present inflationary circumstances, increase the amount of pension which its own employees are receiving, even at the cost of departing from the normal funded features of the plan.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Such payments would not seriously contribute to inflation. The figure of $5 million a year would deal very handsomely with the problem, and inflationary pressures would not be increased at all. That sum would represent an enormous contribution for the welfare of those citizens who have given, in some cases, a whole lifetime of service to their fellowmen by working for the government, people who once thought that their pensions would be adequate and have subsequently found, as a result of inflation which we have not been able to control, that their pension benefits have been eroded.
I also suggest that an exception could be made for pensioners generally. I am inclined to think that it would be very difficult at present to increase old age security pensions across the board in this country. I have not computed what the cost of increasing the guaranteed income supplement would be. Perhaps a strong case would be made for not paying additional benefits. On the other hand, I do not believe that any case can be made for not increasing, on a scale that is tied to the true cost of living, the old age security pension and the guaranteed income supplement. We have just received notice that as of January 1 the old age security pension will become $79.58 a month and the guaranteed income supplement will rise to $111.41 a month. These increases follow the pension index, which in turn follows the consumer price index. Unfortunately, the pension increase does not really follow the consumer price index because the increase is limited to an annual one of 2 per cent. I submit that this is a vicious and unwarranted limitation which, I believe, was unintentionally introduced. I understand that when these pieces of legislation were passed there was little expectation
November 3, 1969	COMMONS
that the cost of living would rise at twice 2 per cent per annum and that this limitation would work hardships on those who are living on pensions. But this has occurred. Since it has occurred, I think the government has the duty to remove this limitation.
Of course, I realize that any pension scheme with benefits which are tied to a rising cost of living is open-ended. If you do not have a limitation in your scheme, it is open-ended. At the same time, however, the government benefits from a rise in the cost of living; its tax revenues increase. The government benefits when incomes rise. Since the government does benefit, it seems to me that on every January 1 there should be no reason for the government not to pass on a small amount of this benefit to those people who otherwise would be left in a very unfair position in our .society vis-a-vis their fellow citizens. Since the government benefits from a rise in the cost of living I submit it should in this small way pay for the consequences of that rise.
I should like to say a few words about Indian policy. The Indian policy which was announced in this House in June by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) is in my opinion a truly liberal statement. It provides for our Indians the goal of equal status instead of the goal of different status. It provides for equality and pledges the government's willingness to provide the means which are necessary if our Indian citizens are to achieve equality. While adopting this fundamental and philosophical principle, the statement elaborates six points and proposes five practical steps which the government will be prepared to take. Nevertheless, despite the undoubted merits of the document the response by the Indian community has been unfavourable. I think we are doing ourselves no service if we believe that the document has been received with anything like overwhelming or even majority support by the spokesmen of the Indians of our country.
It seems to me that Indians disagree little with the principles of equality enunciated in the statement, although no doubt some Indians prefer at present to retain what the statement calls "different" status. Some Indians prefer things to remain more or less as they are; they do not want to make changes. I hazard the opinion that that does not represent the majority view of the Indian community. We are beginning to find a great deal
DEBATES	459
The Address-Mr. MacGuigan of unrest and what may be called agitation in the Indian community, which seems to indicate that our Indians are not satisfied with the status quo but want something better. I believe that Indian response to government statements is based largely on two factors. First, there is an attitude of distrust on their part, a distrust which I fear we have fostered too often in the past with our words and actions. Second, there is fear of a fait accompli according to a strict timetable. We can show rationally that these fears are unjustified, but that will not make them go away.
Recently, while talking with an Indian he expressed the sincere opinion that the white paper on Indian affairs proposed the automatic and immediate abolition of all reserves in this country. From a logical standpoint this is nonsense, because the statement does no such thing; yet this is what my Indian friend took to be the intention after reading the paper or hearing about it. He also believed that the fundamental purpose of the statement was to make Indians rich. He took the position that the aim of the Indians was not to get rich. Again, it seems to me that anyone reading the document would see that this is not so. The principal thrust of the document is this: it does not seek to make Indians rich but to make them free and equal citizens of our country. But because Indians do not trust us, this Indian read the white paper or heard about it and gained these misconceptions about it.
I suggest that we have the responsibility of breaking this deadlock. We, the stronger community, must introduce new elements into the situation which will upset the unfortunate, existing equilibrium. On the one hand we have the policy that is outlined in the government's statement, and on the other we have the response, based on fear, which to a large extent the Indian community has expressed toward the statement. I suggest that we should not push forward our entire plan at this time. We should not urge an over-all approach when we know the Indians have not adopted our philosophy. Instead, we should approach this matter from the other end of the scale.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
We should take a piecemeal approach. We should work on individual projects. Undoubtedly by working on them we would be taking
November 3, 1969

The Address-Mr. MacGuigan steps which would lead toward the goals we have outlined in our white paper. I do not believe we should ask the Indians to accept this philosophy. People may do the same things for different reasons and we should not necessarily expect them, even though we are working on a project co-operatively, to do so for our reasons. We should take a pragmatic rather than a philosophical approach.
I believe the government is beginning to do this. In the last month we have given funds to the Indians to assist them in developing and strengthening their own organizations. This is for our benefit because it ensures that we will talk to people from the Indian communities who will be representative of the views of their communities. But the more direct benefit will accrue to the Indians themselves. It will enable them to set up structures according to their own desires which will enable them to advise us more fully regarding what they want to do. We should continue to give them funds, if necessary even to prepare their own statement on Indian affairs.
I suggest we should proceed with all haste to appoint the claims consultation commissioner mentioned in the government's statement in June. This is very important because the claims consultation commissioner will work with both ourselves and the Indians, advising both groups how to best proceed with regard to Indian treaty and other claims which while not strictly treaty claims have at least a moral status. This appears to be the priority of the Indians.
We take as our priority the philosophical principle of equality, perhaps the basic principle relating to the relationship of the government to the people, the people to the government and generally of man to man. This is not the way in which the Indians approach the problem. The Indians begin by saying: You made certain promises to us and we want to talk about what you will do for us in terms of what you promised. If you do not live up to what you promised in the past, how can we believe anything else you may promise? This view should be placed very high on our priority list. We should proceed as quickly as possible to appoint the mediator between the Indian and white communities to try to solve this very difficult problem and to make concrete suggestions to the white and Indian communities.
The government statement suggests that this commissioner should proceed on a political rather than a legal basis. I believe this is

the soundest approach because regardless of the legal technicalities it is not a subject we can approach strictly in legal terms. That certainly would not satisfy the Indians and probably would not satisfy us.
We are establishing policy for the future; we are not just talking about past treaties. The claims consultation commissioner should have a wide-ranging mandate which would enable him to negotiate and not merely to report on the legalities of Indian treaties. The Indians fear that we mean to suppress them. They need reassurance through deeds and no longer just through words. I believe this is the policy which the government has not only announced but is actually following. I commend the government for its initiative in this area and I urge it to proceed-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will be brief. I wish to say a few words about Parliament. During this Parliament the government has moved effectively to expand executive power, reorganize the cabinet and reorganize a number of departments. It has carried out internal reorganization and is now tightening the administration of departments through its austerity programs. Above all, we see the growing supremacy of the Prime Minister's office and the Privy Council office within the government structure. I applaud all these developments, Mr. Speaker.
However, it is also important to strengthen the legislature, not only as a counterbalance to the executive because of the fear that power may corrupt but for a positive reason. There must be increased participation in government, participation of the public as well as of members of parliament. The public of course cannot always participate directly; they have only rare occasions on which they may do so. They can participate if they are allowed to appear before a parliamentary committee either by being summoned to Ottawa as a witness or by reason of what I hope will become more common, that is, parliamentary committees touring the country and hearing what citizens in different parts of the country have to say about present problems which concern their committees. The
November 3, 1969

same result is achieved through the use of royal commissions, but I believe the government is correct in deemphasizing royal commissions in favour of the full use of parliamentary committees.
In addition to members of the public appearing before parliament through its committees, they also participate symbolically when they see their member of parliament participating in the House or in committees and when they see real dialogue taking place. This is especially true when constituents have expressed their views strongly to their member of parliament and perhaps persuaded him of the urgency of something which he did not previously believe to have high priority. They have the opportunity to see their member make the point in the House or in committee. If they see the representation of their member become policy through legislation or a white paper, they feel a real sense of accomplishment. Even when not all these steps are taken and they see only the process, I believe they are able to share vicariously, through their member of parliament, his participation in government and therefore feel they are participating in a real sense in what is happening in Canada's Parliament.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I am happy to say that the present government has been working strongly in this direction, but there are many more steps which need to be taken. The government has established a legislative committees system in which committees have a genuine, creative, active role in legislation and in studies which lead to legislation, but there is more to be done. Committees need wider-ranging terms of reference. The status of chairmen of committees needs to be upgraded. Committees need a budget for research and for travel so that there may not always be doubt as to the kind of projects in which they can engage. I envisage this as being a small rather than a large budget; if a committee needs more money it should certainly have to come before parliament on each occasion to seek it. There needs to be a reduction in the number of committees and in the membership of committees. There might well be an improvement in the scheduling of committees, perhaps a system of grading into major and minor committees, so that an hon. member serving on a major committee and a minor committee would not have more than one demand made on him at any moment.
The Address-Mr. MacGuigan
Most important, there must be a relaxing of discipline as it affects members of all parties in committee. I realise that members of the opposition point their fingers at the government and suggest it should relax its discipline. It seems to me they do not always bear in mind the effect of discipline in their own parties on members who serve on committees. I suggest that discipline as it applies to members of all parties should be relaxed.
I am confident this is the direction in which the government is moving, and I urge my hon. friends to move rapidly because these are times of rapid change in society and parliamentary institutions themselves are in danger, not only in Canada but in other countries. There is a danger that our policy, our laws for the future, may be made in the streets if they are not made adequately in our legislatures. If they are not made in such a way as not only to be just but to appear manifestly just, they may not be made well enough for the times in which we live.
This is an age in which authority no longer commands respect merely because it is authority. Laws are not respected by reason of their authority so much as by the authority of their reason. I use the word "reason" here not in the more restricted sense in which it was used in the past by philosophers who talked about right reason and doing things properly; it is reason in a manifesting and persuasive sense. We must not only perform well; we must let the people see that we are responding to their needs and deeply-felt aspirations.
I join those who have previously expressed their support for the ideas contained in the Speech from the Throne. I believe it contains a viable and even an exciting program for members of parliament this session and I am sure that with the co-operation of all hon. members we can look forward to a fruitful session of parliament.
